That alone is enough incentive for private companies to begin factoring the KNB’s interests into how they develop and market their products.
Some may argue that the KNB is capable of developing AI models and software itself. It likely is, in principle. But building a competitive AI research capacity from scratch takes years and a talent pool that already has other options – like the private sector with greater pay. Contracting an existing startup with working models is faster, cheaper, and lower-risk than building the same capability in-house. That said, the question is not about the capability per se but is rather about the division of labor. In a booming field like AI, both government and private companies have every incentive to collaborate.
Kazakhstan’s $10 billion data center pact with Nvidia and Firebird, its OpenAI-backed education rollout, and Telegram’s new AI lab at AlemAI are proof of concept. Each shows that Kazakhstani companies and infrastructure can already execute large-scale AI and digital projects credibly enough to attract world-class partners. That track record is itself likely to spur further government funding into the sector, on the logic that money follows demonstrated capacity. 
And as a final twist, the KNB has its own direct stake in that growth: as this infrastructure expands, the agency may well need AI models and platforms of its own – an early warning system to flag threats to a data center, or software to monitor the digital infrastructure it is now charged with protecting – giving it yet another reason to develop and deploy the very technology this piece has described and yet another reason to collaborate with private companies. 
The KNB has emerged as a far stronger actor in Kazakhstan’s AI and digitalization landscape than its low public profile on the matter suggests. For policymakers and civil society, that means factoring a security agency’s institutional interests into a conversation on AI that has so far been dominated by ministries, hubs, and foreign investors. For AI vendors and startups, the new authority cuts the other way: it opens a genuine opportunity to collaborate with a well-resourced government client.
Whether this marks a watershed in and a designing feature of Kazakhstan’s AI economy will depend on how the KNB uses its new powers. The sequencing built into the Decree No. 1258 is itself worth noting. The authority to develop and deploy AI models took effect upon signature, while the KNB’s cybersecurity oversight didn’t take effect until July. That doesn’t look like a purely defensive mandate, and it is precisely the reason why stakeholders across government, industry, and civil society should keep tabs on how the KNB uses its new authority in Kazakhstan’s digital future.
Securitization of digital infrastructure is not new, nor is the involvement of national security agencies therein. These phenomena have become quite common and don’t surprise anyone, especially as cybersecurity threats become more dangerous and sophisticated following the adoption of AI for hostile purposes.
In May 2026, Presidential Decree No. 1258 vested the National Security Committee (KNB) of the Republic of Kazakhstan with additional responsibilities, including in the digital domain. Largely construed as routine modernization efforts, the KNB’s new responsibilities may not have attracted much scrutiny and may have therefore flown under public’s radar, as security agencies worldwide play an increasingly bigger role in cybersecurity. 
Danil Markus is an MA candidate in International Relations and a staff member at KIMEP University in Almaty.
articles.summary: Largely construed as routine modernization efforts, the KNB’s new responsibilities may not have not attracted much scrutiny but they could have significant implications.

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina’s Remarks Spark Bangladesh’s Boldest Message to India Yet
articles.full_text:
Dhaka wants the post-2024 political order to be viewed not only as a domestic transition but also as the basis of a more assertive foreign policy identity.
Bangladesh’s latest diplomatic protest against India is significant not simply because of its unusually strong language, but because of what it reveals about how Dhaka wants its post-2024 political reality — and its relationship with New Delhi — to be understood.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs under the Tarique Rahman-led Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government issued the statement on Wednesday night after former prime minister Sheikh Hasina addressed supporters and the media from New Delhi on the second anniversary of the July movement that led to her ouster in August 2024. 
In her comments, Hasina rejected allegations surrounding the July-August crackdown, defended her government’s actions, criticized Bangladesh’s current leadership, called for the ban on the Awami League to be lifted, and said she planned to return to Bangladesh.
Dhaka responded with one of its strongest diplomatic statements against India since the political transition two years ago. It accused New Delhi of allowing Hasina to use Indian soil to launch “venomous vitriol” against Bangladesh, despite prior concerns conveyed to the Indian government about the possible consequences for efforts to reset bilateral ties.
The Foreign Ministry described Hasina as an “absconding convicted genocider,” a “convicted mass murderer,” and the head of a “mafia enterprise,” while calling her media appearance “an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh” and “a grievous insult to the martyrs” of what it repeatedly referred to as the “July Revolution.”
India, for its part, had earlier maintained that the program was organized by a private entity and that the government neither organized nor endorsed the event or the views expressed there.
But beyond the diplomatic exchange, the statement itself merits closer attention. A careful reading suggests it marks an important evolution in Bangladesh’s official messaging toward India.
Perhaps the most striking feature of the statement was not its criticism of India, but its terminology for the events of July-August 2024. Rather than referring to the “July Uprising” — the phrase more commonly used in official discourse immediately after Hasina’s fall — the Foreign Ministry used the term “July Revolution.”
That distinction is important. An uprising generally denotes a popular revolt against an existing authority. A revolution implies a successful political transformation that establishes a new order.
When such terminology appears in a speech by a politician, it can be dismissed as political rhetoric. When it appears repeatedly in an official statement issued by the Foreign Ministry, it carries greater significance because diplomatic communications represent the position of the state.
By adopting the term “July Revolution,” the ministry statement appears to elevate the events of 2024 from a political episode to a defining moment in Bangladesh’s contemporary statehood. It also signals that the legacy of July 2024 is no longer being framed solely as a domestic political matter, but increasingly as part of Bangladesh’s diplomatic narrative.
Another sentence stands out for its geopolitical significance. “Our people have firmly resolved that our nation will never again go back to the dark days of fascism and that Bangladesh will never be a client State,” the statement said.
The phrase “client State” is rarely found in official diplomatic communications.
In international relations, it generally refers to a country whose policies are perceived to be heavily influenced or shaped by a more powerful external actor. In Bangladesh, critics of Sheikh Hasina’s government had frequently accused the former administration of becoming overly dependent on India in matters of politics and diplomacy.
By incorporating that phrase into an official Foreign Ministry statement, the government appears to be signaling that the political changes of 2024 marked a reassertion of Bangladesh’s strategic autonomy.
That interpretation is reinforced by repeated references throughout the statement to “sovereign equality,” “mutual respect,” “non-interference,” and “national dignity” as the principles guiding relations with India.
Together with the repeated invocation of the “July Revolution,” the message suggests that Dhaka now wants the post-2024 political order to be viewed not only as a domestic transition but also as the basis of a more assertive foreign policy identity.
The statement also reflected a subtle shift in the object of Bangladesh’s criticism. Although it repeatedly condemned Hasina, much of its language was directed at India itself.
The ministry said that Dhaka had warned New Delhi in advance about the possible consequences of allowing the program to proceed, yet India permitted it nonetheless. It also linked the episode to New Delhi’s failure to respond to Bangladesh’s repeated requests to extradite Hasina under the 2013 Extradition Treaty.
In doing so, the statement placed responsibility not merely on the former prime minister, but also on India for providing her political space. That effectively transformed the Hasina issue from one bilateral disagreement into a broader question of trust between the two neighbors.
The statement stopped short of suggesting a breakdown in relations. Indeed, it reiterated Bangladesh’s desire to maintain a “constructive, mutually beneficial, and forward-looking relationship” with India. However, it also made clear that such a reset, from Dhaka’s perspective, cannot be divorced from the Hasina question.
Practical cooperation between the two countries — in trade, connectivity, border management, and security — is likely to continue because both sides have compelling strategic interests in maintaining engagement. Politically, however, the latest statement suggests the relationship is entering a more difficult phase.
More importantly, it indicates that Bangladesh expects its neighbors to engage with the country through the prism of what it has just officially called the “July Revolution” — a political transformation that, in Dhaka’s telling, reaffirmed the country’s sovereignty and ended any perception that Bangladesh could function as a “client State.”
In that sense, the Foreign Ministry’s statement is about far more than one media appearance in New Delhi. It underscores that the debate over Sheikh Hasina is now intertwined with a broader effort to redefine Bangladesh’s political identity, its diplomatic language and the terms on which it seeks to rebuild relations with India.

articles.title: US Pacific Command Considers Moving Billions in Planned Infrastructure Out of Micronesia
articles.full_text:
The U.S. is threatening to pull a $2 billion infrastructure project in Yap. It’s second time recently there have been major problems in U.S. defense negotiations with a COFA partner.
A U.S. Marine Corps F-35B Lightning II prepares for takeoff after receiving fuel from a KC-130J Hercules during an aviation delivered ground refueling as part of exercise Slingshot in Pohnpei, Micronesia June 26, 2026.
Negotiation failures are leading U.S. Pacific Command (PACOM) to look for alternative locations for the $2 billion Department of Defense investment in infrastructure in Yap, Federated States of Micronesia (FSM).   
On June 29, 2026, Admiral Samuel Paparo, the PACOM commander, wrote to President Wesley Simina of FSM that the country’s demand for a “$1.3 billion compensation package is unreasonable, unanchored to demonstrable costs, and divergent from the spirit of our partnership under the Compact of Free Association.”  As a result, “U.S. PACOM intends to move forward by assessing alternative locations across the region to meet the needs of Pacific defense.”
Yap state, made up over a hundred islands, is a core part of the Second Island Chain. The main island in Yap state, also called Yap, is just over 500 miles southwest of Guam. The strategic importance of the Yap group of islands was proven toward the end of World War II. After the United States took the region from Japan, one of Yap’s atolls, Ulithi, became the largest and busiest American naval base in the world.  
FSM’s Compact of Free Association With the U.S.
In the decades after the war, Yap joined with neighboring island groups to form the independent country of Federated States of Micronesia. FSM then signed a Compact of Free Association (COFA) with the United States that ties the two countries together in profound ways, including the citizens of FSM being allowed to live and work freely in the U.S.
Additionally, according to COFA, the “Government of the United States has full authority and responsibility for security and defense matters in or relating to the Federated States of Micronesia.” This goes far beyond usual U.S. defense agreements as it stipulates that this responsibility includes “the obligation to defend the Federated States of Micronesia and its people from attack or threats thereof as the United States and its citizens are defended.”
However, as seen by the latest negotiations, new U.S. defense site access is not guaranteed and requires agreement on terms.  The word “free” in Compact of Free Association has real meaning.
As Howard Hills, former lead counsel and advisor for COFA negotiations under Presidents Ronald Reagan, Joseph Biden, and Donald Trump, explained: “Under COFA the U.S. power to deny military forces of third nations access to the FSM, Palau and Republic of Marshall Islands is absolute and permanent. But to the extent U.S. authority and responsibility for mutual security and defense requires military use and operating rights, that is subject to mutual agreement by the governments concerned, in this case FSM.”  
This is at least the second time recently there have been major problems in U.S. defense negotiations with a COFA country. One reason that Washington pursued Yap airport improvements in the first place was that Department of Defense negotiations for increased access in Angaur, in the neighboring Second Island Chain country of Palau, fell apart. 
There are at least three interconnected reasons this will keep happening unless efforts are made to course correct.
In part because locals see for themselves the comparatively lavish lifestyle of visiting U.S. government officials – often staying the best hotels in town, and eating out every meal – and the relatively astronomical rates given to U.S. consultants and contractors, there is often the perception in FSM that the U.S. government is a bottomless piggy bank. This combines with reporting about the importance of Second Island Chain defenses to give some the feeling they have the U.S. over a barrel.  
There is a pool of lawyers, negotiators, environmental experts, and others keen to fan this perception (and, incidentally, few of them seem to be around when Chinese projects are involved). Given human nature, some local leaders and land owners are drawn to hiring these representatives. In this case, Yap’s negotiators and leaders clearly overreached.  
The $1.3 billion demand comes out to over $185,000 for each of the 7,000 or so resident of the island of Yap. And that amount, combined with the around $1.4 billion appropriated in the NDAA for the Yap airport makes investments in, for example, the airport on the main island of Palau, cost effective. 
Also, at least in the case of FSM, the United States is not necessarily negotiating bilaterally. As made clear in a series of letters written in 2022 and 2023 by then FSM President David Panuelo, the national government of FSM is heavily infiltrated by Chinese political warfare operations – meaning there are some leaders at the national level (at least) with an interest in seeing the negotiations fail.  
As Paparo himself said before the Senate in April 2026, in the Pacific “information, influence, cognitive, and cyber operations achieve increasing strategic effects by shaping perceptions and disrupting decision-making.” This dynamic, combined with corruption, is known to be playing out in FSM.  
Panuelo’s March 9, 2023 letter stated: “One of the reasons that China’s Political Warfare is successful in so many arenas is that we are bribed to be complicit, and bribed to be silent. That’s a heavy word, but it is an accurate description regardless.… What else do you call it when an elected official receives a check for a public project that our National Treasury has no record of and no means of accounting for?”
This means when the United States is negotiating at the national level in FSM, it is likely China has friends in the room. However, there has been no recent public effort by the United States to help the people of FSM liberate themselves from this elite capture, even though it is also affecting U.S. interests. It is possible to do so. 
As a small example, in February, the U.S. Department of State designated some key people in the other two COFA countries, Palau and Marshall Islands. The president of the Senate of Palau, for instance, was called out for “involvement in significant corruption on behalf of China-based actors.”
It’s a good start, with more needed. But not even that much has happened in FSM in spite of a former sitting president of the country calling out his own government for corruption.
As Hills said, “Between scheming PRC agents in the FSM and those who may advise that gouging the U.S. is clever negotiating, let’s hope cooler heads prevail in the national interest of both allies.”
Failure to Understand the Operating Environment
The failure to counter fantasist negotiators with facts or address pervasive Chinese influence is a subset of the more fundamental problem – a U.S. failure to understand local dynamics in FSM. 
Yap’s demand for $1.3 billion is unreasonable. However, the fact some on the Yap/FSM side thought they could get away with it – combined with the failure of the Angaur project and myriad other issues – indicates PACOM has a serious problem with understanding the dynamics on the ground in crucial components of the Second Island Chain. These are places where thousands of Americans died in WWII, including on Angaur and the neighboring Palauan island of Peleliu.
The population of Yap island is around 7,000. Angaur’s is under 150. Yet PACOM’s “Micronesia whisperers” (including in Guam) seem to be missing out on developing relationships with, and listening to, locals who truly understand how things work.  
It doesn’t help that there are no permanent U.S. government officials in Yap – meaning no one locals can get to know, and talk with on a day-to-day basis. Meanwhile, a Chinese state-owned company has set up shop, seemingly permanently. 
Building trust and understanding can’t be done by flying in for a few days, staying in the best available hotels, doing meetings in offices, and relying on AI as well as hamfisted attempts to gain “intel.” On the ground in Yap now, most of the here-today-gone-tomorrow U.S. government officials are thought to be “spies” – a gift to Chinese cognitive warfare operators.
It is possible Paparo’s letter is a negotiating tactic designed to get things back on track. An August 3 letter from President Simina to Yap Governor Francis Itimai acknowledged the “possible setback” and leaves the door open to finding a way forward. 
As Hills put it: “I read the FSM president’s letter to be an opening offer, not a final demand at all, importantly based on apparent initial agreement that the proposed military use and operating rights proposal will strengthen the mutual security and defense alliance.”
articles.summary: The U.S. is threatening to pull a $2 billion infrastructure project in Yap. It's second time recently there have been major problems in U.S. defense negotiations with a COFA partner.

articles.title: As Taiwan’s Drone Budget Debate Drags on, Time Is Running out
articles.full_text:
Taiwan could end 2026 without awarding a single new large-scale contract for domestically produced combat drones.
Taiwan’s government proposed a NT$1.25 trillion (US$40 billion) special defense budget in November 2025 – including its first large-scale procurement of more than 210,000 drones. That was finally passed in May 2026, but with a substantial change: the opposition-led legislature removed all funding for domestically produced drones. In June 2026, the Ministry of National Defense (MND) advanced a NT$210 billion procurement proposal, which led to the introduction of competing bills by each party. 
The legislature finally completed committee review for the budget on July 27, but there was no agreement. The parties could not reach consensus on any provision in their competing bills, leaving all bills intact for further negotiations.
A floor vote could come as early as late August, but if the opposition majority’s version prevails, funding would not pass until early 2027 even under the most optimistic scenario. That means Taiwan could end 2026 without awarding a single new large-scale contract for domestically produced combat drones.
This delay exposes the central danger of the prolonged budget review: Taiwan is falling further behind China’s procurement pace and losing ground as its partners accelerate their own acquisition of uncrewed systems. China has reportedly ordered nearly 1 million drones for delivery by 2026; Ukraine plans to produce 7 million this year; the U.S. Army aims to acquire at least 1 million over the next two to three years; and Japan has allocated 277 billion yen (US$1.7 billion) to rapidly expand its drone arsenal. 
Taiwan’s military, by contrast, holds less than 5,000 drones. A second tranche of 2,032 U.S.-supplied ALTIUS systems has received executive and congressional approval in Washington but remains under contract negotiation, with delivery to Taiwan’s inventory still pending. In an era of drone warfare driven by mass production, testing, and data-enabled software iteration, a one-year procurement gap could prove fatal for Taiwan.
The Budget Debate: Special vs. Annual Budget
Looking back across the debate, one focal point of the dispute between Taiwan’s ruling and opposition parties has been the financing mechanism itself. The ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) sought legislative approval for a five-and-a-half-year, NT$210 billion drone procurement program through a special budget, while the opposition parties proposed procurement through the regular annual budget, paired with additional oversight mechanisms. 
In May 2026, Taiwan’s Legislative Yuan passed the Executive Yuan’s proposed NT$1.25 trillion special defense budget act, but removed approximately NT$470 billion in domestically produced uncrewed-systems funding, cutting the budget to NT$780 billion. In total, 13 bills addressing the excluded programs have since cleared committee review and advanced to cross-party negotiation, but each one has fractured into three party-led versions: from the Executive Yuan/DPP, the Kuomintang (KMT), and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP). The most consequential difference is timing: when each would allow procurement to begin. 
The Executive Yuan responded in June 2026 with a separate NT$210 billion special act covering August 2026 through 2031, designating the MND as competent authority and specifying the purchase of 208,200 littoral attack UAVs, 1,446 littoral surveillance UAVs, and 1,320 small one-way-attack uncrewed surface vessels (USVs). If enacted, this proposal could authorize procurement as early as the end of 2026. 
Opposition parties countered with annual budget alternatives framed around fiscal accountability and legislative oversight, relying on annual appropriations and assigning the Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) the leading role. The KMT version sets a six-year ceiling of NT$240 billion, while the TPP version specifies neither an implementation period nor an overall ceiling. Neither bill identifies platform categories, quantities, or acquisition schedules, and both would push new procurement to 2027 at the earliest. 
Beyond procurement timing, the Executive Yuan separates military acquisition from industrial policy. Its MND-led special budget is built around prioritized operational requirements, while a separate NT$44.2 billion MOEA-led “integrated drone program” for 2025–2030 supports civilian-agency procurement and industrial development. By contrast, the KMT and TPP bills combine technology development, industrial policy, and military drone procurement under a single MOEA-led framework, without specifying how much of the earmarked budget would be allocated to procurement.
Both objectives – urgent procurement expansion and industrial development – are legitimate, but they operate on different timelines. Conflating them has further delayed procurement. 
Annual budget review is not, in most countries, an obstacle to timely defense acquisition. If acquisition plans are clearly defined in advance and the review process allocates funding on schedule rather than deferring it, it can support a country’s prompt procurement. Japan’s FY2026 drone budget was reviewed and passed within roughly two months. The United States’ FY2026 NDAA similarly authorized budgets for uncrewed systems, with congressional consideration completed in about six months.
Taiwan’s current experience illustrates the opposite outcome. Its opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan has created what President Lai Ching-te has called an impasse “unprecedented in Taiwan’s constitutional history.” Taiwan’s annual budget process normally begins with the Executive Yuan submitting its proposal to the Legislative Yuan by late August and concludes by December or January of the same year. Yet the 2026 general budget, submitted in August 2025, was blocked from review for seven months and remains unpassed more than 340 days later – far exceeding the previous record set during the last period of divided government, in 2007. Defense Minister Wellington Koo has therefore warned that the opposition’s use of the annual budget for drone procurement could reproduce this impasse.
If the opposition’s approach is adopted, even the most optimistic scenario – FY2027 budget approval by January – would allow the government to complete its first procurement only by mid-2027. Should FY2027 face the same exceptional obstruction as FY2026, that timeline could slip to late 2027.
Reviewing the rapidly evolving U.S. and Japanese approaches to drone procurement in 2026 offers a useful comparison. They resemble the two models now debated in Taiwan: special budget funding (the United States) and annual budget funding (Japan). Yet the U.S. and Japan share a crucial feature: both operate under multi-year plans with clear procurement targets and rapid implementation, giving industry a more credible long-term demand signal.
In the United States, the Drone Dominance Program has become a flagship defense initiative. Launched under President Donald Trump’s June 2025 executive order, “Unleashing American Drone Dominance,” and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s subsequent directive, “Unleashing U.S. Military Drone Dominance,” the US$1.1 billion, two-year program uses a four-phase competitive process to procure and field approximately 340,000 small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS), including more than 200,000 AI-enabled one-way attack drones by 2027.
This funding comes in addition to the regular annual defense authorization and appropriations process. It is backed by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), a budget-reconciliation measure providing mandatory, multi-year defense appropriations. The law provided US$150 billion in additional defense funding, appropriated in FY2025 and available through September 30, 2029. OBBBA also specifies funding lines for a range of uncrewed capabilities – including small and long-endurance UAS, one-way attack UAS, small and medium USVs, and UUVs.
Why use this reconciliation-funded approach? Hegseth’s rationale was to use immediately available funding to accelerate procurement, create a stable demand signal, and allow industry to build production capacity. As he explained, once the program has strengthened supply chains and manufacturing capacity, “The military services should be able to purchase the drones they need, in the quantities they need and at affordable prices, through regular annual budgets.”
Japan’s drone push, by contrast, relies on annual budgets, but within a defined procurement strategy. Its approach rests on a five-year plan established in 2022, followed by clearly identified procurement programs for FY2026-FY2027 that provide industry with a credible demand signal.
In 2022, Japan adopted its FY2023-FY2027 Defense Buildup Program, which identifies uncrewed capabilities as a priority and envisages approximately 1 trillion yen in investment over five years. Japan’s FY2026 defense budget then allocated 100.1 billion  yen to establish the Synchronized, Hybrid, Integrated and Enhanced Littoral Defense (SHIELD) framework by FY2027, or March 2028. SHIELD covers attack and surveillance UAVs, small USVs and UUVs, and shared control systems, with ten distinct categories of uncrewed systems identified for acquisition.
Japan has also used flexible acquisition mechanisms to accelerate particular capabilities. Drawing on the demonstrated effectiveness of interceptor drones against small UAS in Ukraine, Japan’s Acquisition, Technology, and Logistics Agency launched its Rapid Interceptor Drone Acquisition Program in June 2026. Rather than creating a special legal authority, the program uses existing administrative channels and sets an approximately three-month timeline to select and acquire systems for demonstration trials; any subsequent mass-production procurement will be determined by the trial results.
Taiwan’s debate ultimately comes down to how to create a clear, long-term demand signal while preserving rapid procurement. The United States uses multi-year special funding; Japan uses annual budgets backed by a pre-established multi-year strategy and defined procurement targets. Both have enabled procurement to move quickly.
Both also support industrial development without subordinating military acquisition to it. OBBBA funds industrial capacity while enabling rapid procurement in parallel; Japan separates functions, with the Ministry of Defense leading procurement and the Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry leading industrial policy.
Taiwan need not choose between the two models. It should adopt their shared principle: timely procurement grounded in clear institutional responsibility. Time is running out.

The legislature finally completed committee review for the budget on July 27, but there was no agreement. The parties could not reach consensus on any provision in their competing bills, leaving all bills intact for further negotiations.
A floor vote could come as early as late August, but if the opposition majority’s version prevails, funding would not pass until early 2027 even under the most optimistic scenario. That means Taiwan could end 2026 without awarding a single new large-scale contract for domestically produced combat drones.
This delay exposes the central danger of the prolonged budget review: Taiwan is falling further behind China’s procurement pace and losing ground as its partners accelerate their own acquisition of uncrewed systems. China has reportedly ordered nearly 1 million drones for delivery by 2026; Ukraine plans to produce 7 million this year; the U.S. Army aims to acquire at least 1 million over the next two to three years; and Japan has allocated 277 billion yen (US$1.7 billion) to rapidly expand its drone arsenal.

articles.title: India at a Crossroads: Examining Comprehensive National Power and the Road to 2047
articles.full_text:
Just how powerful is India? CNP may present a better picture than GDP.
Turbulence and conflicts have dominated the first six years of the 2020s. Events like the COVID-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war, and the conflict in West Asia have disrupted the normal way of life across the world. COVID-19 disrupted global supply chains, exposing the vulnerabilities of nations dependent on some others for critical needs. That forced nations to look inwards, focusing on self-sufficiency and self-reliance. The Russia-Ukraine war that followed soon after further exposed key vulnerabilities in global security as well as intertwined issues of trade dependency and connectivity. 
However, the mother of all disruptions has resulted from the war in Iran, leading to closure of sea traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical choke point through which almost 20 percent of world’s crude oil and other petroleum products transit. The conflict is thus causing an unprecedented global energy crisis. 
Yet India has been able to wade through these multiple crises successfully and its economy still continues to grow steadily. India developed a COVID-19 vaccine, which it exported to more than 110 countries. India thus won the trust and respect of the world. 
When the Russia-Ukraine war broke out, it was India’s message that resonated across the globe: “this is not the era of war.” Simultaneously, it withstood pressure from Europe and the United States and continued to buy crude oil from Russia to safeguard its energy security and exercise strategic autonomy.
Amid the ongoing war in Iran, India was quick on its feet to secure supplies of crude oil. As a result, India has successfully diversified its import basket and met its crude oil import requirements of 5 million barrels per day in June and July. 
India is already the world’s fifth-largest economy by nominal GDP. It has one of the world’s largest armed forces, which proved their mettle during Operation Sindoor in May 2025. For the last 12 years across three elections, India has enjoyed political continuity too as it has given mandate to the same political party, the Bharatiya Janata Party. On the diplomatic front, it has expanded its diplomatic footprint across the Global South and has projected itself as its voice and leader. India is also emerging as a critical player in technology, the renewable energy transition, and supply chain diversification. The indicators in public health too have improved significantly over the years and alumni of Indian institutes of high learning like IIT, IIM, and AIIMS are leading global corporations and business. 
So just how powerful is India? To assess these key parameters of national growth and benchmark them collectively, a broader framework called comprehensive national power (CNP) may present a better picture. 
While there is no universally accepted definition of CNP, it is in effect the sum of a nation’s hard and soft power, which cumulatively dictate how much that country can safeguard its national interests and influence global affairs. It can also be assessed in terms of a nation’s ability to mobilize its economic, military, technological, and soft power resources to achieve its strategic goals. 
The Lowy Institute measures CNP through an “Asia Power Index,” which examines more than hundred parameters across eight thematic measures of power: economy, military, resilience, future resources, economic relationships, defense networks, diplomatic influence and cultural influence. For the year 2025, it has ranked India third, behind the United States and China.
The economy has generally been India’s strongest growth parameter in recent times. India is maintaining a steady growth rate of GDP at 6-7 percent, making it the fastest growing major economy in the world. That is driven by India’s renewed focus on manufacturing, innovation, and exports. 
A large consumer market of more than 1.4 billion people helps sustain domestic manufacturing while the operationalizing of free trade agreements is propelling growth in exports and manufacturing. India has set a target of achieving $1 trillion in exports for FY2026-27, with $530 billion in merchandise exports and $470 billion in services exports. This is against a total export of $863 billion last year. 
India’s push for rapid expansion in digital banking and transaction as well as financial inclusion of its marginalized population too is significant. Key tax reforms like the Goods and Services Tax, which have matured over a decade, are adding to government revenues while production-linked incentives including soft loans are propelling jobs and manufacturing across various sectors. A strong foreign exchange reserve, at $600 billion, gives India a cushion against global volatility while an increased push toward making world-class infrastructure like airports, seaports, expressways, etc. is helping overcome huge losses due to inefficient logistics.  
However, these measures will not suffice. Sustained growth of over 7 percent over the next two decades, a focus on manufacturing and exports, self-reliance, smoother logistics and measures to facilitate “ease of doing business” will be crucial for India to realize its economic goals of becoming a developed country by 2047.
Military power is the next significant parameter to measure India’s strength. India has the world’s third-largest armed forces. It is not only the numbers that is making India a military power to notice. Just as important are India’s technological integration and the push toward self-reliance and domestic manufacturing. 
With a tested and fielded “nuclear triad,” a rapidly evolving tri-service military structure, a formidable and diversified missile program, space technology, blue water naval capabilities, and cybersecurity structures, India is a force to reckon with. Modern weapons platforms like the BrahMos missiles, Akashteer air defense systems, hypersonic missiles, and nuclear-powered submarines can help India to project power well beyond the neighborhood. 
The push toward self-reliance and the participation of private industry in defense manufacturing are propelling India’s defense industry. India’s arms exports amounted to almost 390 billion rupees in FY2025-26.
Now India has its eye on future procurements of weapon platforms like fifth-generation fighter aircraft, under terms including transfer of technology, as well as full integration and control over avionics, electronics, and guidance. India is set to emerge as one of the world’s premier military powers. 
However, there are major challenges along the way. India’s defense production and modernization is still uneven and fragmented. The Indian Air Force still runs short in numbers of modern fighter aircraft; advanced technology like aero engines and electronics still need to be mastered. Plus, India’s continued dependence on imports for many significant platforms still compromises strategic autonomy. On top of everything, the unique challenge of a two-front conflict against Pakistan and China poses significant challenges.  
Technology is the next key determinant of CNP. Artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors, quantum computing, biotechnology, cyber capabilities, and space systems are increasingly shaping national power. Fortunately, India has made remarkable progress in several areas. 
India’s Aadhaar, UPI, and digital governance platforms are shining examples of India’s capacity for technological innovation at scale. India’s space program is one of the world’s most modern and advanced. Lunar missions, Mars exploration, satellite launches, and growing commercial space participation have strengthened India’s technological profile. The successful launch of India’s first private space rocket, Vikram-1, by Skyroot Airspace adds more muscle to India’s space program. 
In the field of modern and critical technology, India has already taken steps to promote semiconductor assembly and manufacturing, exploration of critical minerals, and national missions to harness AI and cyber technologies.
However, India still has much to do to catch up with the world’s technology leaders. India has to spend more time and money on research and development. The idea of “sunk costs” has to be accepted for India to develop its own tech platforms like Google, and Microsoft. The startup system in India has to finally end in producing at least a few world level tech companies like Apple, Nvidia, Meta etc. 
The next phase of global competition will be determined by control over advanced technologies. Unless India substantially increases R&D investment, and industrial innovation, its technological CNP will lag behind its economic potential.
Demography and development of human resources is the next big factor in CNP. With a median age of 29 years and 68 percent of the population of working age (15-64 years), India has the greatest demographic advantage in the world, especially at a time when other nations are grappling with a rapidly reducing working population and increasing elderly population. 
How India uses this demographic dividend over the next two decades will be a key determinant of its growth trajectory. Rising numbers of graduates, more numbers taking STEM as a preferred choice in education, and reducing rates of illiteracy point are positive trends. Improved medical services, more hospitals and doctors, reduced infant mortality and maternal mortality along with universal medical cover schemes like Ayushman Bharat are positive indicators in harnessing the true potential of a growing population. However, jobs, social integration, and constructive engagement of the population will be the key to actually making the most of India’s demographic dividend.
Political stability and democratic resilience are yet another strength for India. Over the past 12 years, only one political party has been in power at the center; that has ensured continuity and the ability to pursue long-term reforms in infrastructure, economy, defense, and foreign policy. However, India needs to work around bureaucratic complexities, corruption, judicial delays, land acquisition challenges, and regulatory uncertainty to truly take advantage of political continuity. 
India’s diplomatic influence has significantly expanded over the past decade. That is due to the sum total of progress of everything already discusses: India’s economy, military, technology, and demographics. India’s leadership in global platforms like the G20, BRICS, and Indian Ocean Rim Association has made significant contributions while minilaterals like the Quad and I2U2 (India, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States) have helped India forge focused global partnerships. 
The G20 Summit of 2023, which India presided over, is still counted as the most successful international summit in recent times. India’s effort toward becoming the voice of Global South and its contributions in U.N. peacekeeping missions as one of the largest troops-contributing countries are widely acknowledged too. 
India’s soft power projection is something unique. Almost 35 million Indians are living abroad (including 18 million people of Indian origin) – more than the total population of many countries in Europe. In the Gulf region especially, Indians outnumber most other expatriates, placing them in a significant advantage. However, beyond the numbers and remittances, India has a lot to do to constructively engage with Indians abroad in pushing toward achievements of its national interests.
articles.summary: Just how powerful is India? CNP may present a better picture than GDP.

articles.title: Malaysia Says It Will Not Deport Rohingya if There Are Risks to Their Safety
articles.full_text:
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government has announced plans to repatriate around 5,000 Rohingya with Myanmar’s assent.
An aerial view of a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh.
Malaysia’s government said yesterday that it will not proceed with the planned repatriation of 5,000 Myanmar refugees if their lives are found to be at risk upon their return.
Deputy Foreign Minister Lukanisman Awang Sauni announced recently that around 5,000 Myanmar nationals currently in the immigration detention depot are set to be repatriated as soon as Myanmar is ready to accept them – a fact that Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim confirmed on July 30.
“We have good ​relations with Myanmar. They have now agreed to take 5,000 Rohingya from Malaysia,” Anwar said during a campaign rally in Negeri Sembilan state.
Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil told a press briefing yesterday that the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Home Affairs are currently reviewing the plan to identify the 5,000 refugees to be returned to Myanmar,
“Malaysia, as ​a responsible country, will not return the 5,000 Myanmar refugees if they would ​either be persecuted or their lives would be threatened,” he said, as per Reuters, adding that there were “several matters” that needed to be discussed with the authorities in Myanmar.
“The Prime ⁠Minister has taken note that we cannot send them back if their lives are threatened,” he said. “So there are several matters ​currently being studied by the Foreign Ministry.”
The deportation plan follows a recent upsurge of xenophobic rhetoric and public hostility toward Rohingya Muslims, particularly online. In the past few months, prominent public figures have since described the Rohingya as “criminals” and “intruders” and likened them to a “cancer” on the country, while Rohingya refugee schools across the country ​have been forced to close due to harassment and ⁠threats. Late last month, more than 100 refugees were detained by the authorities after gathering outside the UNHCR building in Kuala Lumpur to ​seek assistance, after being evicted from their settlement in Penang state.
Rohingya asylum seekers have arrived in Malaysia steadily over the past two decades, and particularly since 2017, when an ethnic cleansing campaign by the Myanmar military pushed more than 740,000 from Rakhine State into Bangladesh. They were initially welcomed by their co-religionists, but public opinion has soured in recent years as the population has continued to grow.
Around 126,000 Rohingya asylum seekers are currently registered with the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Kuala Lumpur, around half of the agency’s total. However, Malaysia does not recognize the Rohingya as refugees, and as public sentiment has become more hostile, has tightened the enforcement of its immigration laws. Last month, Malaysia ordered UNHCR temporarily to stop registering new refugees in the country, so that it could begin operating its own system for managing asylum-seekers.
With third-country resettlement becoming more difficult, particularly due to the U.S. government’s new restrictions on refugee admissions, the most likely “solution” is repatriation to Myanmar.
But as human rights groups have pointed out, any proper investigation would conclude that there is little chance that the Rohingya will be able to return home safely. Myanmar’s military-backed government continues to view Rohingya as illegal Bengali immigrants from Bangladesh, and any assurances that it provides about the safety of returnees cannot be taken at face value. In any event, most of Rakhine State is now controlled by the Arakan Army (AA), a Rakhine nationalist group that has also been complicit in attacks on and mistreatment of Rohingya communities.
In a statement earlier this week, the advocacy group Human Rights Watch (HRW) called on Malaysia to suspend the repatriation, declaring that “conditions for safe, dignified, and voluntary return to Myanmar do not currently exist.”
“Malaysia has for many years hosted refugees from Myanmar who have fled unending oppression and atrocities by the Myanmar military,” HRW’s Bryony Lau said in the statement. “The Malaysian government should show regional leadership in responding to the crisis in Myanmar rather than forcibly returning people who are the targets of the junta’s brutality.”

articles.title: Artillery-Missile Command: Vietnam’s Answer to the Maritime-Continental Dilemma
articles.full_text:
Long-range surface-to-surface and ground-based anti-ship missiles will help defend the country on both land and sea.
An air defense gun on display at a military museum in Binh Duong, Vietnam, Nov. 16, 2021.
Vietnam’s military modernization is setting off in a new direction. Instead of procuring naval platforms such as submarines or frigates to defend its South China Sea claims, as it did in the 2010s, the country is looking to upgrade and acquire long-range surface-to-surface and ground-based anti-ship missiles (ASMs) to guard against both continental and maritime threats.
A number of recent developments show that this is the case.
First, Vietnam established the Artillery-Missile Command based on the Artillery Corps in August of last year. The Command was intended to be leaner, given expanded duties, and equipped with more advanced weaponry. Second, it introduced the domestically produced shore-based ASM system Truong Son and showed off the Scud-B tactical ballistic missiles procured from the Soviet Union in the 1980s, on the 80th anniversary of Vietnam’s founding. Hanoi also revealed that it succeeded in upgrading the range of the Scud-B from 300 to 500 kilometers. In May, Vietnam signed a $629 million BrahMos missile deal with India. Third, it is moving the 380th Missile Brigade from Thai Nguyen province in northern Vietnam to Dak Lak province in the Central Highlands, whose mountainous terrain and position at the center of the Indochinese peninsula can help Vietnam project power further southwest in response to security uncertainty from Cambodia. The 380th Missile Brigade is one of Vietnam’s two ballistic missile brigades, along with the 490th Missile Brigade based in Hai Phong in the northeast.
Vietnam’s rationale for this focus on missile forces is rooted in the maritime-continental dilemma. As I argued a few years ago, Vietnam is torn between allocating its resources to the continental west and the maritime east. Land-based platforms such as tanks, artillery, or armored personnel carriers cannot be deployed to defend the country’s outposts in the South China Sea. Frigates, submarines, or patrol boats likewise cannot guard Vietnam’s borders with Laos and Cambodia. Due to resource constraints, Vietnam cannot procure both platforms, and this makes little sense anyway considering that China could easily win an arms race in such a scenario. Vietnam’s air force can defend the two domains, but its Su-22, Su-27, and Su-30 fighters are aging fast. Vietnam has looked to replace its fleet with F-16 and Su-35 fighters, but those deals have not materialized. Vietnam also lacks modern long-range bombers. Missiles thus become the most suitable option for multi-domain deterrence and defense.
Vietnam’s military doctrine is to defend the country early and from afar, and missiles’ long range and quick reaction time fit this doctrine. Importantly, missiles can help resolve Vietnam’s maritime-continental dilemma thanks to their adaptability to multiple geographical domains. ASMs allow Vietnam to prevent an enemy navy from operating in its territorial waters by harassing its naval strike groups. Long-range surface-to-surface missiles can threaten targets in western Indochina or maritime outposts. The fact that these missiles are land-based means they have better survivability compared to frigates or patrol boats, which are exposed on the open ocean. Vietnam’s mountainous and jungle terrain coupled with silos provides the ideal cover for a missile system, while logistics and maintenance lines are more robust on land than at sea. Vietnam’s military has tremendous experience with moving, concealing, and operating missile systems in this terrain from the Second Indochina War. It has also operated Scud-Bs for more than 40 years.
In terms of cost, land-based missiles are cheaper to acquire than single-domain platforms. Vietnam is thus prioritizing the development of ASMs and surface-to-surface missiles. Instead of having to invest in frigates or patrol boats to deny the enemy access to its waters or escort its naval vessels, Vietnam can use land-based missiles for that end. Indeed, it has long counted on the 4K44M Redut-M and K-300P Bastion-P coastal defense missile systems. The development of its own Truong Son coastal defense missile system shows that Vietnam wants to lessen dependence on foreign suppliers and considers land-based platforms an essential part of maritime defense. Missiles also posed an asymmetrical threat to the enemy’s surface warships and aircraft carriers given that each missile is cheap to produce and hard to defend against. Vietnam’s long coastline guarantees coastal missile defense systems can cover most of the South China Sea. Ukraine successfully sank several Russian vessels in the Black Sea using ASMs.
Vietnam’s missiles can be pointed westward too. It is the only Southeast Asian country armed with Scud-Bs. With an upgraded range of 500 kilometers, they allow Hanoi to hit targets throughout most of Indochina from bases in Hai Phong and Dak Lak without having to send troops outside of Vietnam’s territory. Vietnam has test-fired other Scud variants in the 550-700 kilometer range without any issues. BrahMos missiles’ ability to attack both land and sea targets within 300 kilometers only strengthens Hanoi’s strategy of denying enemy access to western Indochina and the South China Sea.
Doctrines and weapons will not be effective without a unified command. And this is why Hanoi decided to establish the Artillery-Missile Command last year. The role of the Command is to streamline the decision-making process and accelerate the kill chain among different military units, including both the ASMs and the surface-to-surface missile units. Due to many provinces having both land and sea borders after the consolidation of 63 cities and provinces into 34 in July 2025, Vietnam seeks to equip each theater of operations with one surface-to-surface missile brigade, one long-range ground-based ASM brigade, and one mixed artillery brigade to give them the versatility to fight enemies from all directions, including from the air. For strategic theaters, Vietnam will allocate even more missile forces. A unified command will ease the process of research and development as well as the adoption of new missile systems throughout all military units. It will also provide the framework for the establishment of future missile brigades.
It is worth noting that while missiles alleviate Vietnam’s maritime-continental dilemma by denying the enemy access, they cannot occupy or reclaim territories. Vietnam will still have to procure single-domain platforms for western Indochina and the South China Sea if it wants to hold physical territories. However, the fact that Vietnam assigns expanded duties to the artillery-missile forces signals that it will not tolerate any gap in defense while it is undertaking long-term weapon domestication for the army and the navy. Hanoi is expected to increase both the quantity and the quality of its missile forces to respond to a multi-threat environment under a porcupine strategy.

articles.title: Vietnam to Build Memorial to North Korean War Dead Outside Hanoi
articles.full_text:
The memorial will be built at an existing ⁠cemetery that commemorates 14 North Korean fighter pilots shot down while battling the U.S. Air Force in the late 1960s.
The Revolutionary Martyr’s Cemetery outside Pyongyang, North Korea.
Vietnam’s government plans to build a memorial to the North Korean soldiers who perished during the Vietnam War, state media announced this week, casting a rare light on the country’s role in the conflict.
According to a Reuters report that cited Quan Doi Nhan Dan, a newspaper published by the Ministry of Defense, the memorial project was discussed at a meeting chaired by Deputy Defense Minister Nguyen Truong Thang ​in Hanoi on Monday. Also in attendance was North Korean ​Ambassador Ri Sung Guk.
“The ⁠Party, State, people, and People’s Army of Vietnam always cherish and remember the effective assistance of North Korea and the sacrifices of North Korean martyrs in its struggle ​for national independence ​in the ⁠past,” Quan Doi Nhan Dan quoted Thang as saying, according to the news agency.
The memorial will be built at an existing ⁠cemetery for North Korean ​“martyrs” in the northern province of Bac Ninh outside Hanoi, the report said. The cemetery contains headstones commemorating 14 North Korean pilots, including two officers, who were sent to support the North Vietnamese air force during its war against the U.S.-backed South Vietnam in the 1960s. The headstones face northeast, in the direction of Korea. The cemetery is also set to be refurbished under the Defense Ministry’s plans.
The downed pilots were part of a group of around 100 that North Korea dispatched to North Vietnam to train their Vietnamese counterparts in the mid-1960s. One Vietnamese veteran told VnExpress in 2019 that the pilots were then invited to “fight alongside Vietnamese soldiers.”
They flew Soviet-made MiG-17 jets in combat missions ​against U.S. aircraft during the late 1960s, and the 14 North Korean pilots were killed between September 1965 and early 1968, according to a state media report.
The airmen were among the estimated 1,000 North Koreans who were secretly sent to North Vietnam between 1966 and 1971. They included mechanics, support personnel, psyops specialists, and engineers.
For years, the role of the North Korean army in the Vietnam War was veiled in secrecy. While the DPRK supplied North Vietnam with military and political support during the war, including by sending North Korean military advisers to the country, it wasn’t until 2000 that a Vietnam official openly admitted that North Koreans had played an active part in the conflict. North Korean state media only officially confirmed its involvement in 2001, saying that the country had sent weapons, ammunition, and 2 million sets of uniforms.
The decision to actively support North Vietnam was made in 1965, and endorsed by a meeting of the ruling Workers Party the following year. Before the pilots’ departure to North Vietnam, President Kim Il Sung told them “to fight thinking of Vietnam’s sky as your own sky, Hanoi as Pyongyang and Ho Chi Minh as your own leader.”
The North Korean admission took place shortly before Kim Yong Nam, then North Korea’s second-most-senior leader, visited Vietnam in July 2001, during which he paid his respects at the cemetery in Bac Ninh. The remains of the dead pilots were then repatriated to ​North Korea in 2002, but the headstones remain in place, facing northeast – the direction of Korea – alongside a memorial marker that reads, “Here used to lie 14 North Korean comrades.”
The North Korean contribution to the communist cause in Vietnam paled in comparison to South Korea’s support for the southern Republic of Vietnam. In total, around 320,000 South Koreans fought alongside U.S. troops to defend the south, and more than 5,000 died.
The North Koreans dispatched to Vietnam never came into direct contact with their South Korean brethren, but psychological warfare personnel targeted South Koreans with communist propaganda and anti-American leaflets. “South Korean soldiers in Vietnam! Seek hundred, thousand vengeances against the American imperialist aggressors!” read one.
Despite their wartime cooperation, relations between Hanoi and Pyongyang grew chilly in late 1978, when Vietnam invaded Khmer Rouge-ruled Cambodia, another recipient of North Korean aid. The relationship was then further damaged when Vietnam established diplomatic ties with South Korea in 1992.

The memorial will be built at an existing ⁠cemetery for North Korean ​“martyrs” in the northern province of Bac Ninh outside Hanoi, the report said. The cemetery contains headstones commemorating 14 North Korean pilots, including two officers, who were sent to support the North Vietnamese air force during its war against the U.S.-backed South Vietnam in the 1960s. The headstones face northeast, in the direction of Korea. The cemetery is also set to be refurbished under the Defense Ministry’s plans.
The downed pilots were part of a group of around 100 that North Korea dispatched to North Vietnam to train their Vietnamese counterparts in the mid-1960s. One Vietnamese veteran told VnExpress in 2019 that the pilots were then invited to “fight alongside Vietnamese soldiers.”
They flew Soviet-made MiG-17 jets in combat missions ​against U.S. aircraft during the late 1960s, and the 14 North Korean pilots were killed between September 1965 and early 1968, according to a state media report.
The airmen were among the estimated 1,000 North Koreans who were secretly sent to North Vietnam between 1966 and 1971. They included mechanics, support personnel, psyops specialists, and engineers.
For years, the role of the North Korean army in the Vietnam War was veiled in secrecy. While the DPRK supplied North Vietnam with military and political support during the war, including by sending North Korean military advisers to the country, it wasn’t until 2000 that a Vietnam official openly admitted that North Koreans had played an active part in the conflict. North Korean state media only officially confirmed its involvement in 2001, saying that the country had sent weapons, ammunition, and 2 million sets of uniforms.
The decision to actively support North Vietnam was made in 1965, and endorsed by a meeting of the ruling Workers Party the following year. Before the pilots’ departure to North Vietnam, President Kim Il Sung told them “to fight thinking of Vietnam’s sky as your own sky, Hanoi as Pyongyang and Ho Chi Minh as your own leader.”
The North Korean admission took place shortly before Kim Yong Nam, then North Korea’s second-most-senior leader, visited Vietnam in July 2001, during which he paid his respects at the cemetery in Bac Ninh. The remains of the dead pilots were then repatriated to ​North Korea in 2002, but the headstones remain in place, facing northeast – the direction of Korea – alongside a memorial marker that reads, “Here used to lie 14 North Korean comrades.”
The North Korean contribution to the communist cause in Vietnam paled in comparison to South Korea’s support for the southern Republic of Vietnam. In total, around 320,000 South Koreans fought alongside U.S. troops to defend the south, and more than 5,000 died.
The North Koreans dispatched to Vietnam never came into direct contact with their South Korean brethren, but psychological warfare personnel targeted South Koreans with communist propaganda and anti-American leaflets. “South Korean soldiers in Vietnam! Seek hundred, thousand vengeances against the American imperialist aggressors!” read one.
Despite their wartime cooperation, relations between Hanoi and Pyongyang grew chilly in late 1978, when Vietnam invaded Khmer Rouge-ruled Cambodia, another recipient of North Korean aid. The relationship was then further damaged when Vietnam established diplomatic ties with South Korea in 1992.
Vietnam’s government plans to build a memorial to the North Korean soldiers who perished during the Vietnam War, state media announced this week, casting a rare light on the country’s role in the conflict.

articles.title: Are India and Indonesia Leaving the Non-Aligned Movement Behind?
articles.full_text:
Rather than signaling the abandonment of non-alignment, the same principles are increasingly pursued through a different set of institutions.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi (left) and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto visit the Prambanan Temple Compound Restoration and Conservation Project in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, Jul. 8, 2026.
When Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Jakarta last month, the joint statement issued by India and Indonesia addressed almost every major strategic issue facing Asia. It highlighted the Indo-Pacific, BRICS, ASEAN, maritime security, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, resilient supply chains, and cooperation among the Global South. Yet there was no reference to the Non Aligned Movement (NAM), despite India and Indonesia being among its founding members and the leaders whose cooperation at the 1955 Bandung Conference helped lay its intellectual foundations.
The NAM was similarly absent from the joint statement issued during President Prabowo Subianto’s visit to India in January 2025. The disappearance of the NAM offers a window into how two of Asia’s most important middle powers now understand strategic autonomy. Rather than signaling the abandonment of non-alignment, the same principles are increasingly pursued through a different set of institutions, partnerships, and diplomatic priorities.
India and Indonesia have long occupied a unique place in the history of postcolonial diplomacy. The Bandung Conference articulated principles of sovereignty, anti-colonialism, peaceful coexistence, and independent foreign policy that later shaped the establishment of the NAM in 1961. During the Cold War, these ideas provided newly independent states with a framework for resisting pressure to align with either Washington or Moscow while asserting a greater voice in international affairs.
But the strategic environment that gave rise to non-alignment no longer exists. The central challenge facing Asian middle powers today is not simply avoiding military blocs. It is preserving policy autonomy while navigating an increasingly complex landscape shaped by great power competition, economic interdependence, technological rivalry, and overlapping regional institutions. Strategic autonomy has therefore become less about standing apart from the international system than about participating in it on one’s own terms.
That evolution is clearly reflected in the India-Indonesia partnership. Rather than centering the relationship on the language of non-alignment, the two countries frame their cooperation through a dense network of contemporary frameworks, including ASEAN, BRICS, the G20, the Indian Ocean Rim Association, and overlapping conceptions of the Indo-Pacific. In building up their ties, India and Indonesia have placed equal emphasis on defense industrial cooperation, maritime domain awareness, artificial intelligence, digital connectivity, critical minerals, and resilient supply chains. These priorities represent a different way of pursuing national resilience and strategic flexibility. Strategic autonomy has become increasingly issue-based rather than institution-based.
During the Cold War, the NAM served as the principal political vehicle through which many developing countries expressed their independence. Today, India and Indonesia pursue the same objective across multiple platforms simultaneously. ASEAN reinforces regional diplomacy. BRICS expands cooperation among emerging economies. The G20 provides influence over global economic governance. Indo-Pacific initiatives address maritime security and connectivity. Rather than relying on a single movement, both countries increasingly assemble strategic autonomy through overlapping partnerships.
Importantly, the principles associated with Bandung – sovereignty, territorial integrity, international law, peaceful dispute settlement, and a stronger voice for the Global South – have not disappeared. These are ideas deeply embedded in the diplomatic traditions of both countries, but those principles are now expressed through different means.
This distinction matters beyond India and Indonesia. Across Asia, middle powers are adapting to a strategic environment that is simultaneously more interconnected and more contested than the Cold War order. Few seek exclusive alignment with any single major power. Instead, they cultivate diversified relationships across security, economic, and technological domains while preserving room for independent decision making. Strategic autonomy has become an exercise in managing multiple partnerships rather than avoiding them.
Seen in this light, the disappearance of the NAM from India and Indonesia’s recent joint statements should not be interpreted as evidence of its demise. The movement continues to exist, and many of its core principles remain relevant. What appears to be fading is its role as the primary diplomatic framework through which those principles are articulated.
India and Indonesia continue to defend the values that once inspired the NAM. But they increasingly do so in the language of ASEAN centrality, “a free, open, transparent, rules-based, peaceful, prosperous and inclusive Indo-Pacific,” BRICS, and the Global South rather than the NAM itself. The legacy of Bandung therefore lies not in the continued invocation of a Cold War institution, but in the enduring pursuit of strategic autonomy under the conditions of a very different international order.

articles.title: Has Life in North Korea Changed Since 2013?
articles.full_text:
The author of “Witness to North Korea” reflects on which lessons from his time in the country are still relevant today.
Vitamin A distribution in North Korea in the early 2010s.
Last month, as I launched my new book “Witness to North Korea,” conversations with Wall Street Beijing Bureau Chief Jonathan Cheng and NK News’ Alannah Hill brought up one important question: is this memoir of my three years living and working as the United Nations Resident Coordinator in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) still relevant to the North Korea of today? 
I wrote this book for anyone wishing to understand, as Stimson Center Fellow Frank Aum wrote, “what it actually means to engage with the DPRK – not in the abstract language of policy briefs, but through the granular, often maddening, reality of day-to-day diplomacy and humanitarian work.”
This question of continued relevance between what I observed then and the country today is a valid one. After all, I left Pyongyang in 2013 – and yes, things in the country have changed since my departure. Some North Korea experts talk of a rising middle class with cash to spare, of one mobile phone subscriber for every three North Koreans, of ski resorts – all thanks to the phenomena of marketization and monetization changing the up-to-now closed economy and forcing the hand of the North Korean regime to open to international trade. 
Another thing has changed: data has become even harder to obtain. In 2020, North Korea used the COVID-19 pandemic to deny entry to several EU-member countries that had kept an embassy in Pyongyang and to most of the international community’s assistance programs. These embassies and resident U.N. agencies, as well as most international NGOs, have not yet returned. The U.N. population census remains, to this day, an essential source of quality data about North Korean society. Sadly, there has not been such an exercise since I left 13 years ago.
My discussions with U.N. officials and humanitarian organizations point, today, to a continuation of the underlying problems that I describe in my book, which continue to shape the lives of ordinary North Koreans. Kim Jong Un’s regime continues to experience a gap between intention and reality in four major areas: food and nutrition; public health and infectious disease; availability of medicines and medical equipment; and, finally, technical cooperation and capacity building. These problems concern both domestic limitations and international constraints.
During my years in Pyongyang, the United Nations and many NGOs worked with North Korean institutions to improve agricultural production, strengthen health services, support maternal and child nutrition, conduct the national population census, and assist vulnerable communities facing chronic shortages. These efforts were based on a simple reality: despite its political isolation, the North Korean population faced genuine needs that could not be solved through sanctions or diplomacy alone.
Kim Jong Un’s unusually candid admission last February that agricultural production remains inadequate and that decades of rural policy have failed echoes many of the concerns that humanitarian agencies encountered during my posting. While today the emphasis has shifted toward livestock production, dairy farming, and regional development, the objective remains the same: providing sufficient and nutritious food to a population that continues to experience chronic shortages. 
During my time in North Korea, workplaces and factories would allow their people to leave during the day to forage in the hills, as the government acknowledged the persistence of a “food problem.” Today, the North Korean government’s ambitious rural modernization program reflects an acknowledgement that food security is still a national challenge rather than a problem of the past.
The health sector presents an equally familiar picture. Authors Joon Hee Han and Yo Han Lee, in a deeply researched January 2026 article titled “North Korea’s 2025 Health Revolution,” found that while North Korea is investing heavily in new hospitals and health infrastructure, questions remain about foundational input such as medicines, trained personnel, reliable electricity, and sustainable financing. 
Similarly, during my time in Pyongyang, we repeatedly found that physical infrastructure alone could not guarantee improved health outcomes without parallel investments in equipment, pharmaceuticals, professional training, and institutional capacity. All indications suggest that, aside from the usual showy investment centered on Pyongyang, this lesson remains as relevant as it was when I visited health centers around the country from 2009 to 2013.
Many reports point to a shift in international aid from Russia, and away from Europe and the United States. And yet, the issues the country faces remain unchanged. A Russian court ordered more than 30 North Korean nationals to undergo tuberculosis treatment in Moscow in 2024 and 2025, according to court documents, belatedly confirming both North Korean labor flows into Russia and a suspected infection outbreak among overseas workers.
During my assignment to Pyongyang, tuberculosis was already recognized as one of North Korea’s most serious public health challenges, and international cooperation played an essential role in diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. The prevalence of the disease over a decade later highlights the well-known problem of continuing weaknesses in disease detection, treatment and public health capacity in North Korea – and the continuing importance of international health cooperation.
Finally, aside from North Korea’s unwillingness to receive technical assistance from the United Nations, NGOs, and a few bilateral donors, current international restrictions continue to make international engagement difficult. Engagement is neither a concession to the regime nor an endorsement of its policies. It is a practical means of empowering individuals while creating channels of communication in an otherwise isolated country. 
The recent debate over sanctions exemptions, NGO licensing, and restrictions on humanitarian operations demonstrates that this question remains unresolved. If anything, international assistance organizations today face even greater operational obstacles than during my tenure.
Yet international technical cooperation continues to matter. International agencies connect North Korea to the world through a variety of interventions such as civil aviation coordination, vaccination programs, or drug control – albeit within limits and constraints due to their reduced ability to implement and monitor their programs on the ground. 
These developments reinforce one of the principal conclusions from my time in the country: technical assistance to North Korea should not be viewed as a political reward but as a means to support the North Korean people. Isolation has not eliminated North Korea’s needs. Instead, it has often made it more difficult for international organizations to respond effectively to them.
The regime is not a static monolith. Parts of the leadership, aware of structural weaknesses, attempt significant reforms in agriculture, health care, and regional development. International assistance should support them, not by replacing domestic responsibility but by providing expertise, resources, and technical cooperation where they are most needed.
The dilemmas I described in “Witness to North Korea” – how to balance sanctions with humanitarian principles, how to engage without legitimizing the regime, and how to reach vulnerable populations while respecting international law – will shape the work in Pyongyang and the international community’s posture toward North Korea. The details have evolved, but the fundamental questions remain consistent.
For readers seeking to understand whether international engagement with North Korea still matters, the answer emerging from both my experience and these recent developments is clear. The country’s population continues to face serious challenges, and sustained, principled, smart engagement remains one of the few practical means of improving the lives of ordinary North Koreans while preserving channels for dialogue in one of the world’s most isolated states.
