articles.title: When the World Stops Fearing the Bomb
articles.full_text:
On the 81st anniversary of the bombing of Japan, the hibakusha are disappearing just as fast as the world is becoming numb to their cause
The wrecked framework of the Museum of Science and Industry in Hiroshima, Japan, shortly after the dropping of the first atomic bomb, on Aug. 6, 1945.
Terumi Tanaka was 13 when on one fine day the sky above Nagasaki was suddenly flooded with blinding white glare; “a blazing inferno” he would recall years later. At 97 now, he still carries memories of sitting next to the window. His home was hit suddenly by a flash, then thunder, followed by an unbearable silence. Within moments, his city was reduced to ash. 
“It was literally hell,” he said in his eyewitness account.
With the average age of the hibakusha (atomic bombing survivors) reaching 87, there will soon be no one left to provide such first-person testimony.
As humanity loses these eyewitnesses — 91,105 left as of March 2026 — we are also losing our moral compass. As the world commemorates the 81st anniversary of the dropping of atomic bombs on Japan, a cruel irony is fast unfolding in front of our eyes. The generation that witnessed the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings is fading away just as the world rediscovers the strategic significance of nuclear weapons — and loses sight of the human suffering such weapons embody.
For decades, the horrors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki had imposed an invisible restraint on policymakers. Nuclear weapons were tolerated, but never celebrated. The nuclear taboo — non-possession, non-transfer, and non-use of nuclear weapons — was assumed to be universal and robust. Today, deterrence has displaced disarmament as the dominant concern. Even before the last hibakusha leave this earth, the world is turning its back on their warnings.
The nine nuclear-armed states possess 12,241 nuclear warheads, with nearly 9,614 retained in military stockpiles. This is certainly better than 70,300 warheads in 1986 when Russia and the United States possessed more than 90 percent of the world’s nuclear bombs. Driven by their detente of 1970s and the end of Cold War from late 1980s, the Soviet-U.S. (and later Russia-U.S.) arms control agreements had really shrunk their arsenals. But with all nuclear-armed states now busy with modernizing their nuclear weapons, that trajectory of arms control has begun to reverse.
China has expanded its stockpile the fastest: from 350 warheads in 2022 to 620 in January 2026. The United States and Russia are investing hundreds of billions of dollars in next-generation delivery systems. Britain plans to raise its warhead ceiling, while France is upgrading its sea-based deterrent. More worrying still, nuclear doctrines are lowering the threshold for potential use. In India, where it was long assumed that its warheads stayed de-coupled from their launchers, SIPRI this year reported that 12 nuclear warheads had been actively deployed as its sea-based deterrent. Nuclear weapons are no longer regarded as weapons of last resort; they are steadily becoming instruments of routine statecraft. 
This transformation marks the collapse of the post-Cold War belief that nuclear weapons were gradually becoming politically less valuable. Instead, great power rivalry, especially since the start of the Ukraine war, has revived the centrality of deterrence discourse. With the expiry of the New START Treaty on February 5, 2026, the United States and Russia no longer have any legally binding bilateral nuclear arms control treaty limiting their nuclear arsenals.
Equally revealing is what has happened to disarmament discourse. The Chemical Weapons Convention, negotiated in the early 1990s, was the last disarmament treaty successfully concluded through traditional inter-state mechanisms. Since then, the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva — the world’s sole standing multilateral negotiating forum on arms control — has remained paralyzed. 
Civil society organizations have since stepped in to fill the vacuum. Their efforts produced the Ottawa Convention banning anti-personnel landmines, the Convention on Cluster Munitions, Arms Trade Treaty and, eventually, the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. However, this last one is neither signed nor ratified by any one of the nine nuclear weapon possessing nations.
Few regions illustrate this reversal more starkly than Europe. During the Cold War, millions marched in streets under the banners of the Nuclear Freeze Movement and the European Nuclear Disarmament campaign. Following the collapse of the Berlin Wall, abolitionist optimism inspired initiatives ranging from the Canberra Commission to the Global Zero movement. Europe was seen as the moral custodian of arms control and strategic restraint.
Today, strategic anxieties have displaced that moral conviction. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and growing uncertainty over the United States’ long-term security guarantees have transformed Europe’s strategic imagination. Britain and France, Europe’s two nuclear states, are modernizing their arsenals. French President Emmanuel Macron has openly proposed extending France’s nuclear umbrella to European partners, while Germany and several NATO members are actively debating expanded nuclear-sharing arrangements. 
Europe — the intellectual birthplace of post-war arms control and confidence building measures — is quietly reinventing itself as the laboratory of nuclear reassurance. The Hague summit of NATO last year pledging all members raising their defense budgets to 5 percent of GDP has further accelerated the process of militarization.
Europe’s trajectory is concerning, but Washington’s approval of a long-term civilian nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia marks the most recent profound shift in global non-proliferation politics. By contemplating uranium enrichment capabilities on Saudi soil while accepting less-than-ideal bilateral safeguards, the agreement blurs the distinction between civilian nuclear cooperation and latent weapons capability. 
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has already declared that his Kingdom would pursue nuclear weapons should Iran acquire them. Riyadh recently signed a mutual defense pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan, whose defense minister is on record saying that Pakistan’s nuclear arsenal “will be made available” to Saudi Arabia if needed. 
This is proliferation in the 21st century. It advances not through clandestine enrichment facilities hidden beneath mountains – the model pursued by North Korea and Iran – but through carefully drafted agreements, strategic partnerships, and diplomatic communiqués. The world’s nuclear future is being negotiated in conference rooms, with the results announced proudly in public. 
What makes this transition dangerous is not merely the growth of nuclear arsenals but the shrinking of public alarm. Stockpile expansions, modernization programs, and shifting nuclear doctrines now receive less global attention than financial turbulence or celebrity controversies. The bomb has not become safer; the world has become numb to its dangers. That is precisely what the hibakusha spent eight decades warning against. 
The terrifying testimonies of hibakusha nursed humanity’s moral immune system for the past 81 years. They reminded governments that behind every discussion of deterrence and doctrines lie families and generations that will be erased in seconds. Their lived memories restrained policymakers more effectively than treaties ever can. Yet they will soon be gone.
As Terumi Tanaka’s generation walks into the horizon, another generation is learning about Hiroshima and Nagasaki as two modern metropolises. If the 20th century taught humanity how terrifying nuclear weapons could be, the 21st risks teaching us something even more dangerous – that Hiroshima and Nagasaki survived, even came to thrive. The implication is that nuclear weapons are no more than instruments of statecraft. 
A repeat of the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki remained unthinkable all this time not because the world commemorated it as an annual ritual, but because the presence of hibakusha reminded us why it should never happen again. Those witnesses are running out of time. But the world may already have stopped paying attention.

With the expiry of the New START Treaty on February 5, 2026, the United States and Russia no longer have any legally binding bilateral nuclear arms control treaty limiting their nuclear arsenals.
articles.summary: On the 81st anniversary of the bombing of Japan, the hibakusha are disappearing just as fast as the world is becoming numb to their cause

articles.title: Why Asia Is More Enthusiastic About AI Than the West
articles.full_text:
In China, India, much of Southeast Asia, and elsewhere in Asia, the net benefits of AI are perceived by populations to be greater than their drawbacks.
We are living in the age of artificial intelligence (AI). AI dominates the headlines, spreads its influence into all spheres of life, and is increasingly seen as vital to the economic growth and national security of nations. The use of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude have become ubiquitous in daily life. Needless to say, the increased spread of AI — and its impact on relationships, employment, and other facets of society — has provoked trepidation among many.
However, surveys consistently show that Asians — and in fact, most non-Western populations — are much more enthusiastic and excited about AI than people from the West. According to a survey conducted by Ipsos in 2025, over 80 percent of respondents from the Southeast Asian countries of Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Singapore said that AI will profoundly change their lives in the next few years. Eighty-four percent of Chinese respondents said that products and services using AI excited them. Likewise, 65 percent of Indians, 67 percent of Turks, and 69 percent of South Koreans felt the same way, compared to 38 percent of Americans, 31 percent of Canadians, 37 percent of the British, and 40 percent of the French.
Whilst Japan was an outlier in the Ipsos survey, with 46 percent of Japanese respondents indicating that they were excited about AI, in a separate survey by Pew, only 28 percent of Japanese respondents said that they were more concerned than excited about AI. Similarly, only 26 percent of people from Turkiye, 21 percent from Israel, 19 percent from India, and 16 percent from South Korea felt more concerned than excited about AI. Contrast this with half of Americans responding that they were more concerned than excited about AI.
There is therefore a clear and noticeable difference between Asian — and other non-Western populations — and Western attitudes toward AI that invites an explanation. There are several reasons why Asians are more enthusiastic about AI than Westerners.
First, AI improves the life of an average citizen of an Asian country relative to any downsides that it may have. AI is seamlessly integrated into a wide number of day-to-day activities such that it feels like an ordinary part of life, or a tool to improve life, rather than as a threat. In China, for example, where trust in AI is among the highest in the world, AI is embedded in many government services and private payment tools, so using it is unavoidable. According to Chinese journalist Nina Xiang, Chinese users tend to be pragmatic in favoring convenience over privacy when it comes to AI use.
In more advanced societies, such as Japan and South Korea, AI is useful for increasing productivity and performing tasks in economies with aging populations and falling birth rates.
Even more importantly, AI is extremely useful in places where educational, bureaucratic, and professional services are scarce or substandard, as is the case in many parts of India. In many villages, schools are often understaffed, with a single teacher teaching dozens of children whose learning styles may wildly differ. AI is useful in this scenario and preferable to the alternative of not learning, because it can tailor explanations and exercises to each individual’s abilities. AI also compensates for weak institutions or helps individuals manage difficult tasks in a multilingual country with a difficult bureaucracy. Contrast this with Western countries, most of which have relatively efficient and functional governments that may not immediately require streamlining by AI, or the internet more generally. For example, India developed the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) system to deliver welfare directly to Indians rather than routing benefits through corrupt middlemen. AI has helped streamline this process.
Furthermore, AI is significantly less disruptive to societies in which white-collar workers form a smaller percentage of the population. Most Western states have a higher proportion of white-collar workers than the rest of the world. The long development, over time, of the liberal arts and sciences in a collegiate or post-graduate environment ensured a large supply of quality teachers, researchers, lawyers, writers, and scientists who rely on working with texts and information. In short, the West gains from AI less, at least in the short term, given the structure of its economy and education system, along with its level of development. Correspondingly, Western societies also have more to lose from the disruption caused by AI. An LLM model may provide a poor child in Bihar with the best English teacher he has ever had but may put a struggling associate lawyer or a writer in New York City out of a job.
Second, Asians see AI, and technological progress in general, as key to national greatness, economic development, and a brighter future. AI is not something to get queasy about or starve of funding. Beyond prosperity, there is also an element of geopolitical calculation in countries like China. In China, there is a pervasive narrative that ties technology to national development and holds that China’s past inability to keep up with the West led to its century of humiliation, during which technologically superior Western states with gunboats and rifles imposed their will on China.
According to Natalia Cote-Muñoz, a former official in the U.S. State Department, the consensus view in Chinese public discourse is that China will advance while the West is starting to stagnate because of the increasing hostility toward AI among many in the West. Very few Chinese individuals are worried about potential job losses because they believe that the government will find a way to apply the technology and insulate against widespread unemployment. In short, Chinese citizens understand that China is rising, the future will be better than the present, and that technology will play a key part in all this, which is the opposite of how many Americans feel about the direction that technology is taking.
Finally, many Asian philosophical traditions are less antagonistic toward AI. In the traditional religions of many Western societies, humanity is set above — and aside from — the other creations of God, such as animals and plants, as well as its own tools. In this worldview, recently expressed by Pope Leo XIV, the special nature of humanity itself may be threatened by machines that mimic the human mind. As a result, robots and other AIs are often seen as threats and rivals, something often reflected in movies and novels.
In Western imagination, the development and use of AI could be seen as a classic example of the Faustian bargain, whereby someone trades their soul or humanity for power, wealth, and knowledge. The Chinese government would reject this line of thought, because it sees AI as a useful tool like any other, one to be regulated, controlled, and aligned with its core values.
Many Asian religions and philosophies also see intelligence and awareness as characteristics of a number of beings, not limited to humans. In some schools of Hinduism, for example, jivas, or souls, inhabit several creatures. These range from plants to devas or gods. Human beings exist along a spectrum of consciousness between these two extremities. Japanese Shinto also believes that the world is filled with kami or spirits, who may inhabit a number of inanimate and animate objects. Other schools of Hinduism, such as Advaita Vedanta, hold that the entire universe is conscious. Likewise, Daoism asserts that everything in the universe is made of qi, or energy. Finally, Buddhism believes that all mental experiences are the result of a stream of processes made up of aggregates called skandhas, which again, are not limited to human beings.
As a result, the traditional cultural and philosophical underpinnings of Asian thought are less primed to believe the Western notion that AI is fundamentally different to or opposed to humanity and the essence of the human spirit. In many schools of thought in Asia, the boundary between mankind and all the rest of existence is less rigid than in Western philosophy and religion. Many Asian philosophies view AI as a part of the natural world, and thus something humanity can interface with, like other phenomena, such as animals and gods. While many Asians may not be explicitly aware of these philosophical points, the underlying ideas resonate with their culturally shaped worldviews, and could play a part in influencing their enthusiasm toward AI.
Asians are more enthusiastic about AI because AI is not seen as a threat, as something that will make the future worse, poorer in both spirit and in personal wealth. articles.title: China’s World AI Cooperation Organization Agenda
articles.full_text:
China’s President Xi Jinping delivers opening remarks at the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai, China, July 17, 2026.
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Gloria Chen – head of Asia-Pacific geopolitical strategy and business development at Rocky Road Resilience, a U.K.-based specialist risk advisory – is the 520th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Analyze China’s agenda behind the World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO).
The World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) was founded in Shanghai this July, with founding members including Russia, Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Pakistan, virtually all BRICS members except India, plus a number of other Global South countries, with no major Western democracies among its members. China positions it as an “intergovernmental organization” and claims to aim for the “beneficial, safe, and fair” development of AI. 
Just as Christian civilization shaped Western culture and ways of thinking, the deeply rooted Confucian culture of China has similarly shaped the Chinese value system and language system. Confucian culture emphasizes moral correctness and face-saving, and is centered on family culture. From the perspective of the Chinese regime, China is very clear about what kind of “correct” language to use to legitimize its actions. Looking at the 2026 World AI Conference (WAIC), China tells you it wants global cooperation, AI regulation and world prosperity. However, the manifestation of family culture is often: “I tell everyone I’m promoting the common good, but what I really want is to make my family prosperous and for me to become a leader.” 
Because of resource monopolies, long-term wars historically, and internal struggles, Chinese leaders have a deep-seated insecurity. Therefore, they believe that only by seizing power and controlling others can they secure their own safety. As a result, this nation finds it difficult to cooperate with others. WAICO’s abbreviation differs from the United Nations’ World AI Organization (WAIO) by only one character. Those familiar with Chinese culture know that names always have special symbolic significance for China. So I think China’s WAICO agenda is to gradually establish a China-led AI hegemonic empire.
What does the composition of the 29 WAICO signatories reveal about China’s agenda?
The WAICO strategy aims to build an organization of non-Western democratic systems led by China and to co-opt specific regimes. One of its strategic objectives is to connect regimes isolated by the international community, such as Russia, Cuba, and Myanmar, and to influence and control their political situations through financial aid and AI technology. 
China provides “unconditional aid” through the Belt and Road Initiative, mobilizing vast amounts of national wealth and resources to support partner countries. This model will also appear in WAICO, with the strategic goal of maintaining relations with Global South countries to gain diplomatic leverage and extend China’s sphere of influence. China can exert influence in distant regions through AI technology and infrastructure, potentially even involving destructive activities. 
To gain legitimacy for its global expansion, China attempts to package the organization’s purpose as benefiting impoverished countries and the world, portraying Western countermeasures as hegemonic suppression. China then seizes the narrative through social media platforms like TikTok and YouTube, making young people and the middle class in Western democracies believe that the CCP is a victim of suppression and a true peace advocate, thus tearing Western societies apart and weakening democratic countries from within (a strategic tactic that China excels at). 
Compare and contrast China-led WAICO to U.S.-led Pax Silica Initiative.
From Xi Jinping’s speech at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC), we can analyze the main goal of WAICO’s establishment, anti-monopoly and anti-injustice, is essentially China’s effort to build its own AI hegemony by uniting with Global South countries to break through Western technological blockades. This is China’s core objective. All the other nice-sounding words China utters, such as equality, openness, and mutual benefit, have already been said during China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Instead of listening to what the Chinese say, it’s better to observe their actions.
The United States’ Pax Silica, on the other hand, is a typical democratic capitalist initiative, emphasizing cooperation and supply chain security, and deepening economic partnerships among democratic countries. After all, for democratic countries, mutually beneficial economic cooperation under international free trade creates the greatest national interest. 
Although current narratives often equate the U.S. with hegemony, democratic countries are fundamentally different from authoritarian states. Private enterprises and entrepreneurs remain a significant force in democratic societies, and democratic elections give citizens a certain degree of voice. Alliances among democratic countries are still built on trust, technological cooperation, and shared values, which is drastically different from the absolute dominance of authoritarian hegemony and its opposition to free trade.
If we continue to simply portray China and the United States as two superpowers vying for hegemony, we are likely to fall into the linguistic trap set by China. This kind of argument misleads people into portraying China and the United States as similar countries. However, the United States is a democratic country and China is a dictatorship, and they are fundamentally different in nature. 
Examine how WAICO advances China’s geopolitical ambitions. 
WAICO can be seen as China’s AI version of the Belt and Road Initiative. Both follow similar paths, and one of their strategic objectives is to connect non-democratic regimes like Russia and Cuba that are not integrated into the international community. Their shared goal is to counter U.S. pressure and establish opposing camps in international geopolitics, using WAICO as an organizational tool for China to extend its sphere of influence. 
The Belt and Road Initiative’s strategic objective is to build an “axis of evil” against Western democratic values ​​through monetary diplomacy and alliances with authoritarian regimes. This same strategic objective is also reflected in WAICO. The difference lies in the inclusion of China’s advantageous AI capabilities, shifting the competitive landscape beyond the manufacturing and high-tech industries where China has historically struggled against the West. 
Assess the role of WAICO in intensifying the China-U.S. AI race and its implications for AI sovereignty and governance.
China possesses advantages in the AI ​​industry that Western countries lack. In the past, China struggled to truly surpass Western technology at the forefront of innovation. However, in the AI ​​industry, which heavily relies on databases and testing personnel, China boasts a much larger pool of testing personnel and unparalleled data compared to the West. 
According to the “Statistical Report on Internet Development in China,” as of December 2025, China had 1.125 billion internet users and 602 million generative AI users, representing a 141.7 percent increase in AI users compared to the end of 2024. This has created one of the world’s largest training data pools, providing a powerful impetus for model development and optimization. This massive scale enables Chinese developers to conduct large-scale AI training and inference faster than most other countries, and to further test, improve, and deploy artificial intelligence systems 
Furthermore, the Chinese government has the authority to rapidly and centrally invest its highly monopolized resources in the AI ​​industry, devoting all its efforts to strengthening computing power, algorithms, and data infrastructure. This speed and resource allocation model is difficult for Western democratic governments to achieve. A report released by the China Internet Network Information Center (CNNIC) shows that as of the end of December last year, China’s generative AI computing power exceeded 1590 quadrillion calculations per second. Data from the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) shows that China has become the world’s largest holder of AI patents, accounting for as much as 60 percent. 
China has placed artificial intelligence at the core of its economic strategy and, through the establishment of WAICO, is actively promoting the creation of an international system to regulate the use of this technology. By leveraging its ever-growing AI capabilities, China seeks to dominate the AI ​​regulatory system, a part of its efforts to reshape the international order. This is not merely about the AI ​​industry; it’s about overthrowing Western liberal values ​​and reshaping a new world order. This is China’s fundamental strategy. 
At this year’s WAIC, Xi Jinping stated, “We should formulate laws and regulations, technology monitoring, early warning, and emergency response systems to ensure that artificial intelligence always remains under human control.” Xi also expressed opposition to prioritizing the security of one nation over the security of others in the field of AI. 
While these statements are politically correct, their essence is that China wants to seize control of the discourse and leadership in AI regulation. In other words, China wants to decide how AI can be used and how it can answer questions, much like China’s “DeepSeek,” always avoiding sensitive political issues. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which rose to power through propaganda, understands that AI will be the search engine and encyclopedia of the new era. Only by controlling the AI ​​regulatory system can the CCP write its desired historical narrative. 
Maintaining power and achieving global dominance are China’s core strategic goals in AI. For China, the arrival of the AI ​​era represents its only historical opportunity to defeat the West, what Xi Jinping calls “seizing historical opportunities.” 
At the WAIC, Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI launched its powerful new flagship model, Kimi K3. Other highlights included MiniMax’s M3 model and Huawei’s Atlas 950 “super node.” Compared to the closed systems of American giants OpenAI and Anthropic, an increasing number of foreign companies, such as Siemens, and numerous Silicon Valley engineers are adopting Chinese open-source AI models due to their performance, low cost, and the customization features. If Western countries cannot stop this trend, the increasing use of Chinese AI models by Western companies and AI professionals will create another form of supply chain hijacking.

articles.title: Kim Yo Jong Warns Japan Over First Tomahawk Missile Test
articles.full_text:
The powerful sister of North Korea’s leader said Japan’s preemptive attack capability is entering the “stage of the actual act.”
The Japanese destroyer Chokai fires a Tomahawk missile on July 29, 2026. It was Japan’s first live-fire test of a Tomahawk.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, warned on August 5 that Pyongyang would set up additional military options against Japan. The statement followed the first live-fire test of a Tomahawk cruise missile by the Japanese navy. The missile was launched from the Aegis destroyer Chokai in the Pacific Ocean, on July 29. 
“Japan, a war criminal state, is accelerating its transformation into a war state, taking advantage of the acute and variable trend of the present international situation in which global geopolitical conflicts and inter-camp confrontation are getting fiercer,” Kim said in her statement, which was published by the North’s state-controlled Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). 
She cited the test-firing of the U.S.-supplied Tomahawk missile by Japan, along with Tokyo’s participation in a U.S.-led joint military drill in the Philippines in May. Those moves prove that Japan’s push for preemptive strike capability has entered “the stage of the actual act,” according to Kim.
Japan’s pursuit of long-range strike weapons dates to December 2022 when Tokyo revised three key security documents to adopt what it calls “counterstrike capability,” a shift away from its decades-old policy of maintaining a strictly defensive military. The revision, described at the time as Japan’s biggest military buildup since World War II, opened the way for its purchase of 400 Tomahawk missiles from the United States, deliveries of which began this year.
Kim said that “Japan’s moves to formulate the possession of the capability for preemptive attack” were “contrary to international law and its constitution, which disallowed the possession of war potentials, the right to participate in a war and the right to belligerency.” She added: “The mass possession of different kinds of long-range strike means with an unexpectedness of preemptive attack and a drastic increase in the radius of their operation and their deployment of multi-demesne forward spaces for actual war, including sea, underwater and air, make Japan reorganize its overall armed forces as a formation of preemptive attack and overseas aggression.”
Japan has said its military buildup is necessitated by what Tokyo calls the “most severe and complex security environment since the end of World War II.” Ironically, Japan claims its new capabilities are motivated in part by North Korea’s own actions. In its latest defense white paper, Japan’s Defense Ministry warned that “North Korea’s military activities pose an even more grave and imminent threat to Japan’s national security than ever before.”
For North Korea’s part, Kim said Tokyo has long postured as a “peace-loving state” while branding neighboring countries’ own defense measures as “threat” and “provocation.” She called that posture “a camouflaged tactic to cover up its ambition for a military giant.” While accusing Tokyo of building up its military capabilities to threaten her country, Kim also blamed Washington for enabling the test. 
“I make it clear upon authorization that the armed forces of the DPRK and the military leadership will set up additional military options which are obviously due to Japan’s transformation of these days,” Kim said.
Kim did not disclose further details about the “additional military options” Pyongyang is planning.

articles.title: 15 Months After Massacre at Pahalgam, Terrorists Target Non-local Civilians Again in Kashmir
articles.full_text:
Two laborers from central India were shot dead at a brick kiln in Kulgam in the Kashmir valley on July 31.
A year of relative calm in the Kashmir valley was shattered on July 31 when terrorists opened fire on two non-local laborers at a brick kiln in Kilam village of South Kashmir’s Kulgam district. The two laborers were migrants from the central Indian state of Chhattisgarh.
The attack at Kulgam has triggered panic among tens of thousands of laborers from India’s poorer northern states, who come to the Kashmir valley every year between March and November to work on construction sites, road projects, brick kilns, and apple orchards. The July 31 killings prompted some of them to return home.
The Kulgam attack came close on the heels of the killing of a Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) police constable at a busy market in Anantnag district. The attacks have raised concern over the return of terrorism to the Kashmir valley.
Indeed, the incident at Kulgam is the first targeted killing of non-local civilians by terrorists since April 22, 2025, when 26 men, all civilians, were shot dead at Pahalgam; 25 of them were from outside J&K and one was a Kashmiri pony ride operator, who tried to stop the shooting.
The massacre at Pahalgam led to India launching Operation Sindoor targeting terrorist camps and infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir, which culminated in a four-day war between India and Pakistan in May. There had been no attacks on civilians since then; the bloodletting over the past fortnight broke that lull.
The killings at Kulgam came days before the seventh anniversary of New Delhi’s abrogation of J&K’s autonomy. It was on August 5, 2019, that the Narendra Modi government announced the revocation of Article 370 and Article 35A – a unilateral action that was hugely unpopular in J&K. India will also be marking its 79th Independence Day on August 15. The run-up to anniversaries of milestone events usually sees an uptick in terror attacks in the Kashmir valley.
Since August 2019, over 25 non-local workers have been killed in terror attacks in Kashmir. In October that year, six laborers from West Bengal were lined up and shot dead in Kulgam. There were 10 migrant laborer fatalities in 2022. A terror strike on a construction team working on the Z-Morh tunnel in Ganderbal district resulted in the death of six migrant workers and a Kashmiri doctor in October 2024.
The post-2019 surge in attacks on non-local workers can in part be attributed to Delhi’s nullification of Article 35-A, a constitutional provision that preserved the distinct identity of J&K.
Kashmiris were apprehensive that the scrapping of Article 35-A would “open the floodgates to non-locals to work and live in the valley, altering the local demography and allowing outsiders to get jobs here,” a Kashmir University professor told The Diplomat. Terror groups “capitalized on these anxieties” to kill scores of non-local laborers working in J&K, she said.
Officials in India’s security establishment attribute the attacks on non-local workers to the success of the Modi government’s crackdown on terrorists and separatists. The number of active local militants has fallen in recent years and the network has shrunk somewhat.
Under those circumstances, militants “opt for attacks on civilians, who are soft targets. Such attacks are not only easier to carry out, but they are low-cost and have high impact,” a senior official of the Central Reserve Police Force told The Diplomat. Especially when these attacks result in “fatalities of non-locals, it gets immense media coverage, helps the terror outfit remain relevant and keeps their handlers across the border [in Pakistan] happy,” he said.
“By targeting non-local laborers, terrorist groups seek to spread fear, discourage investment and developmental activities, disrupt the inflow of outside workers, and challenge the perception of normalcy that has gradually returned to J&K in recent years,” Ajit Kumar Singh, senior fellow at the Institute for Conflict Management, wrote on the South Asia Terrorism Portal.
Citing security officials, journalist Zulfikar Majid wrote in the Deccan Herald that “the recent terrorist attacks in the Kashmir valley do not indicate a major resurgence of militancy.” Rather, the “insurgency [is] adapting to weakness rather than demonstrating renewed operational capability,” he argued.
Following the attack at Pahalgam last year, tourism in J&K was hit hard. Non-local workers in the valley were badly rattled. In spring this year, the laborers returned, as did the tourists, expecting a safer environment. The attack at Kulgam has made the migrants fearful again.
In response, Indian security forces launched a massive manhunt and tightened the security cordon in the valley. Surveillance and night patrolling have been stepped up. But keeping workers safe may be easier said than done.
There are thousands of migrant laborers in the valley. Some have brought along their families. “What we plan to do is move them and their families to a single location in the same village for the night, so that it is easier to secure them,” a police officer told Indian Express.
But creating non-migrant clusters could make them more vulnerable.
Establishing Kashmiri Pandit (Hindu Kashmiris) clusters or townships has often been put forward as a way to draw back this displaced community, which was forced to leave the valley in 1990. The idea was a non-starter, one reason being that such clusters would make the Pandits sitting ducks for Islamist radicals.
Non-local clusters could also be targeted by militants opposed to J&K’s economic recovery. The government will have to act fast to create an environment where migrant workers feel safe to avert their flight from the valley.

articles.title: What a Near-Miss Drone Incident Reveals About South Korea-US Operational Coordination
articles.full_text:
South Korea’s army thought they were locked on to a North Korean UAV. It actually belonged to the U.S. Marine Corps.
U.S. Marines employ a Stalker VXE30 Unmanned Aerial System during a Combined Arms Live-Fire Exercise at Rodriguez Live-Fire Complex, South Korea, March 5, 2026.
On July 30, air defense units along South Korea’s front line in Paju, Gyeonggi Province, detected an unidentified aerial track on a thermal observation device (TOD) and local air defense radars. Assessing the object as a potential airborne threat, the South Korean Army Ground Operations Command immediately issued “Durumi,” a high-alert air defense posture triggered in response to suspected enemy unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) incursions. For 90 minutes, anti-aircraft gun systems and attack helicopters were placed on emergency standby in a state of high tension.
However, the unidentified object was not an infiltrating North Korean drone. It was a Stalker (VXE30) reconnaissance UAV operated by the U.S. Marine Corps, conducting an exercise nearby as part of the Korea Marine Exchange Program (KMEP).
While a friendly-fire incident was narrowly averted, the implications are profound. Severe vulnerabilities exist in both asset management and inter-ally command-and-control communication mechanisms along the Korean Peninsula.
A closer look at the sequence of events underscores systemic operational flaws. Prior to the exercise, U.S. forces had notified South Korean military counterparts of their flight plans and formally dispatched official documentation. Yet, this critical information stalled at the working level within the South Korean military bureaucracy; it was neither briefed upward to senior command nor disseminated down to frontline units.
Remarkably, South Korean Marine Corps personnel were actively participating in the joint exercise alongside their U.S. counterparts. Despite operating under the same airspace during a combined exercise, essential flight data was never shared with key frontline formations responsible for border defense, such as the South Korean Army’s I Corps. Operational communication across service branches – between the Army and Marine Corps – and across the alliance suffered a complete breakdown.
The Ministry of National Defense’s initial attempt to characterize the incident as a simple clerical error or administrative oversight misconstrues the fundamental issue. Frontline air defense is a critical component of national security where delay or error carries high risks. An incident in which a U.S. military asset was nearly targeted by South Korean air defense systems highlights real-world gaps in operational coordination and information sharing between the two allies.
At its core, alliance interoperability depends on mutual trust and real-time command-and-control capability. If basic procedures for real-time situational awareness and friendly force identification fail during routine exercises, the effectiveness of combined South Korea-U.S. forces in a complex crisis scenario comes into question. The breakdown in border airspace communication reflects broader operational inertia and exposes vulnerabilities in tactical compatibility.
Rather than dismissing the event as an isolated incident, military leadership must conduct a comprehensive review of air defense operational procedures and combined asset-sharing mechanisms. Holding individual working-level personnel solely accountable will not prevent similar misidentifications in the future. Preventing recurring risks along the border will require structural reforms in information dissemination and combined airspace management procedures.

articles.title: When Small States Practice Buddhist Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
While China and India compete for influence through Buddhism, smaller states such as Bhutan and Singapore are showing how Buddhist values, networks, and heritage can be transformed into diplomatic influence.
Their Majesties the King and Queen of Thailand, accompanied by His Majesty King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck and Her Majesty Queen Jetsun Pema of Bhutan, attended a Buddhist chanting ceremony at the Buddha Dordenma statue in Bhutan on April 26, 2025.
As strategic competition between China and India intensifies, Buddhism has become an increasingly visible instrument of foreign policy. China has positioned itself as a center of Mahayana Buddhist civilization, sponsoring international Buddhist forums, restoring sacred sites, and weaving Buddhist heritage into its Belt and Road Initiative. India, the birthplace of Buddhism, has promoted its own Buddhist heritage by expanding pilgrimage circuits and lending sacred relics abroad.
The focus on China and India obscures a quieter, yet equally significant, story. Buddhist diplomacy is being practiced not only by Asia’s largest powers, but also by two of its smallest states: Bhutan and Singapore.
The cases of Bhutan and Singapore demonstrate how small states can pursue Buddhist diplomacy under different conditions. Their limited geopolitical weight and lack of great power status have encouraged them to cultivate influence through cultural networks and regional cooperation.
Bhutan, the world’s only official Vajrayana Buddhist kingdom, is a small, landlocked Himalayan state that has placed Buddhist values at the heart of both its domestic governance and its engagement with the world.
This approach owes much to the vision of the Fourth King, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, who developed Gross National Happiness not simply as an alternative measure of development, but as a strategy for reconciling modernization with the preservation of Bhutan’s Buddhist culture and national identity. For a small state situated between India and China, this fusion of Buddhist values and development also served a strategic purpose, turning cultural distinctiveness into a means of safeguarding sovereignty while giving Bhutan an international profile far beyond its size.
The current king, Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck, has had to navigate the structural constraints of Bhutan’s position between two much larger powers, preserving its longstanding ties with India while cautiously managing a consequential relationship with China, with which Bhutan still has no formal diplomatic relations. Against this backdrop, cultivating close relations with Thailand, Southeast Asia’s leading Theravāda Buddhist monarchy, provides Bhutan with a valuable partnership beyond its immediate geopolitical neighborhood.
Bhutan’s relations with Thailand have been reinforced through a series of recent high-level royal exchanges, including King Vajiralongkorn’s historic state visit to Bhutan in April 2025, King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck’s receipt of an honorary doctorate from Chulalongkorn University in December 2025, and his attendance at the funeral rites of Princess Bajrakitiyabha in June 2026. In these exchanges, Buddhism serves as a shared cultural and symbolic language through which the two Buddhist monarchies deepen their bilateral relations.
The ongoing Gelephu Mindfulness City project extends Bhutan’s Buddhist diplomacy into the economic realm, transforming mindfulness, sustainability, and well-being from ethical principles into a distinctive national brand for attracting global investment and talent. In doing so, however, Gelephu exposes a central tension in Bhutan’s development strategy: Buddhist values that caution against excessive materialism are being strategically mobilized to facilitate the country’s deeper integration into global capitalism.
Unlike Bhutan, Singapore is a secular, multireligious republic with no official religion. Singapore therefore does not ground its diplomacy in Buddhist kingship or religious identity. Instead, it has cultivated a role as an intermediary, using Buddhist heritage to facilitate dialogue among governments, religious communities, scholars, and cultural institutions. This reflects Singapore’s broader diplomatic strategy as a small state: rather than competing directly with larger powers, it has sought to enhance its relevance by positioning itself as a connector among them.
Some of Singapore’s most effective Buddhist diplomacy has taken the form of people-to-people diplomacy, exemplified by the late Venerable Hong Choon, whose extensive ties with Thailand earned him the title of Supreme Chinese Monk from King Bhumibol Adulyadej and enabled him to host Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn during her visit to Singapore. He simultaneously cultivated extensive networks in China, making repeated visits and building relationships with senior Buddhist and political leaders throughout the 1980s, before Singapore and China established diplomatic relations in 1990.
During his tenure as Singapore’s foreign minister, George Yeo represented another dimension of this story. He championed the revival of Nalanda University as part of an “Asian Renaissance” that sought to recover Asia’s shared civilizational heritage as a basis for contemporary regional cooperation. A Catholic deeply engaged with Asian philosophies, Yeo demonstrated how Buddhism can transcend religious affiliation to become a diplomatic resource, enabling a small, multireligious state like Singapore to position itself as a connector among Asia’s larger powers while advancing regional dialogue and educational cooperation.
Singapore’s museums have likewise emerged as important actors in Buddhist diplomacy, using exhibitions of Buddhist material culture not only to strengthen institutional partnerships across Asia but also to position Singapore as a site for the interpretation and circulation of the region’s shared heritage. The upcoming Dunhuang exhibition at the Asian Civilizations Museum, organized in collaboration with the Dunhuang Academy in China, is a case in point, illustrating how Buddhist art can move beyond aesthetic appreciation to become a medium of cultural diplomacy that fosters regional relationships and advances Singapore’s role as a cultural connector in Asia.
As China and India continue to compete for influence across Asia, Bhutan and Singapore reveal how Buddhist diplomacy can operate in strikingly different small-state settings. 
In Bhutan, a Buddhist kingdom, Buddhism is embedded in the monarchy, national identity, and statecraft; in secular and multireligious Singapore, it functions instead as one among several cultural resources available for building regional connections. 
This contrast suggests that small-state Buddhist diplomacy has no single model: its effectiveness lies precisely in its capacity to adapt Buddhist actors, material culture, and networks to different political and cultural contexts while advancing national interests.

articles.title: China’s ‘Internet Addiction’ Schools Are Now Locking Up Adults
articles.full_text:
Parents are paying institutions to coerce adults whose life choices conflict with family expectations.
In March, a 21-year-old music student in Beijing arrived at an apartment complex to teach a piano lesson. Waiting for her were her father, her aunt, and two employees of a private disciplinary institution. Her relatives told her the strangers were police officers investigating a family matter. Instead, they forced her into a vehicle, confiscated her phone, and drove her hundreds of miles to an institution in Henan province, where she spent the next 11 days.
According to Southern People Weekly, her parents objected to her romantic relationship and believed their once-obedient daughter had become difficult to manage. They paid the institution to isolate her, monitor her daily life, and pressure her into ending the relationship. Public reporting indicates that this institution charged 26,800 yuan (around $4,000) for six months or 36,800 yuan for a year, including room and board.
The incident reflects a broader transformation in an industry once associated almost exclusively with treating so-called “internet addiction.” A July investigation by China Newsweek documented several adults placed in similar institutions by their own families. One 21-year-old man said his parents paid for a facility to “correct” his sleeping habits. A 25-year-old woman living alone reported being taken from Jiangxi to a disciplinary institution in Hubei after relatives and staff entered her home and confiscated her phone. Another investigation by Jiemian News found adults as old as 33 living alongside teenagers in one behavioral correction school.
These institutions emerged during the 2000s, amid national anxiety over youth “internet addiction.” Many gained notoriety for military-style discipline and physical punishment before public criticism pushed the industry to rebrand as family education centers, behavioral intervention programs, or youth development organizations. The name has changed; the business model has simply expanded to adults whose life choices conflict with parental expectations. Romantic relationships, gaming, unemployment, unconventional careers, and irregular sleeping habits can all become reasons for intervention.
China’s Criminal Law makes it a crime to unlawfully deprive another person of personal liberty, punishable by up to three years in prison. A June commentary in The Beijing News made the point bluntly: a contract authorizing “military-style management” is not a valid defense. If its terms conflict with the law, the outlet argued, the contract itself is void – no matter how much paperwork a family signs beforehand.
In practice, enforcement tells a different story. Lyu Jin, who had turned to gig work delivering food after being laid off, was intercepted by five men his mother had hired after he failed to meet her expectations of “stable employment and marriage.” He flagged down police at a highway checkpoint while being transported to a facility in Chongqing; officers stopped the vehicle but released it after his escorts produced an authorization letter signed by his mother. Lyu Jin is an adult; his parents had no legal basis to sign away his rights. But the police let them do it anyway.
Legally, adulthood in China begins at 18; parents have no authority over where their adult children live or whom they date. Socially, and evidently in the eyes of some local police, parental responsibility is often understood to continue well past that threshold, especially for only children in whom families have invested heavily. The law is applied differently if a parent, rather than a stranger, is the one arranging the involuntary confinement. 
That is where these institutions find their market. They sell forms of control that parents can no longer exert over their adult offspring: transportation, isolation, restricted communication, tightly controlled daily routines, and constant supervision. In effect, parents are paying these institutions to force their children to acquiesce to their demands.
As long as a signed parental contract can function, in effect, as a shield against prosecution, these institutions will keep expanding to justify whatever behavioral “corrections” parents want made.

Instead, they forced her into a vehicle, confiscated her phone, and drove her hundreds of miles to an institution in Henan province, where she spent the next 11 days.
According to Southern People Weekly, her parents objected to her romantic relationship and believed their once-obedient daughter had become difficult to manage. They paid the institution to isolate her, monitor her daily life, and pressure her into ending the relationship. Public reporting indicates that this institution charged 26,800 yuan (around $4,000) for six months or 36,800 yuan for a year, including room and board.

She covers gender, digital culture, and social change in contemporary China, She is also a contributing writer to Global Voices. She holds an M.S. in Global Affairs from New York University and a B.A. in Translation from The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen. Get in touch with Lina by LinkedIn or email.
articles.summary: Parents are paying institutions to coerce adults whose life choices conflict with family expectations.

articles.title: Russia’s New Move in the Kuril Dispute
articles.full_text:
Moscow is naming one of the disputed islands after a Soviet spy who operated in Imperial Japan.
A bust honoring Richard Sorge in Kazan, Russia.
The planned naming of a disputed Kuril island after Richard Sorge is the latest example of Russia strengthening its control over the features. It is part of a decade-long effort by Moscow to use commemoration to reinforce its claim regardless of Tokyo’s protest. 
On July 28, the Sakhalin branch of the Russian Geographical Society announced the future placement of a plaque for Sorge, a Soviet intelligence officer, on an uninhabited island in the Lesser Kurils. Moscow is expected to rename the island after Sorge soon.
The announcement drew attention in Japan given the island’s location and Sorge’s legacy.
The island is part of the disputed Southern Kurils, which Japan calls the Northern Territories. The Kuril Islands stretch from Hokkaido to the Kamchatka Peninsula and provide Russia with protected access from the Sea of Okhotsk to the Pacific. Soviet forces occupied the islands in 1945, just before Japan’s surrender ended World War II. Japan still claims the southernmost four features: Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan, and the Habomai Islands. More than 80 years later, the dispute remains unresolved.
Richard Sorge remains a consequential figure in Japan and Russia.
Disguised as a German journalist, Sorge led a successful espionage network for Moscow in Tokyo from 1933 until his arrest in October 1941. A close friendship with German Ambassador Eugen Ott and partnership with Japanese journalist Ozaki Hotsumi gave Sorge unmatched access. Ott’s confidence gave him insights into the German-Japan alliance. Ozaki’s ties to Prime Minister Konoe Fumimaro’s inner circle gave Sorge access to information from the highest levels of the Japanese government. The network layered political information with military activity to validate details, increasing the reliability of their reporting.
During the summer of 1941, Sorge’s network provided Moscow with information on Japan’s internal debate over whether to widen World War II in the Pacific. Their reports confirmed Tokyo would advance south into Southeast Asia in late 1941 rather than invade the Soviet Union.  
The actual events were more nuanced than the popular narrative. The July 2 Imperial Conference produced an intentionally ambiguous policy that preserved both northern and southern options while masking unresolved Army-Navy rivalry. Sorge’s reporting mixed Ozaki’s accurate assessment with less reliable information from a German military attaché. The result was a message that was broadly correct, if less clear-cut than later accounts suggest. 
Over the next three months, Sorge’s network steadily strengthened the case that Japan had adopted a southern-facing strategy by tracking halted railway conversion orders, stalled troop concentrations, and a decline in Kwantung Army mobilization pressure. Their intelligence, combined with signals intelligence and information from other networks, aided Moscow in moving forces from Siberia to defend the capital.
Russia celebrates Sorge as a hero and master intelligence officer. In Japan, he represents a costly intelligence failure and a reminder of the environment surrounding the decision to expand the war in 1941. 
Sorge wasn’t always feted in Moscow, however. Soviet authorities denied Sorge for two decades; Josef Stalin even refused to intervene before Sorge’s execution in 1944. But in 1964, Nikita Khrushchev named the late Sorge a Hero of the Soviet Union. The decision followed renewed interest sparked by mass culture during an era of de-Stalinization. President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly cited Sorge as an influence on his decision to join the KGB.
Naming the island after Sorge links Russia’s territorial claim to a Soviet wartime achievement. It also invokes a period that remains sensitive in Japan.
Russia has previously sought to tie Sorge to the disputed Kurils. In January 2022, Moscow proposed exhuming Sorge’s remains in Tokyo and reburying them on one of the disputed Kuril Islands.
Rather than moving remains, the current proposal attaches Sorge’s name directly to the island, creating another marker of Russia’s claim.
Moscow previously named various features in the Kurils in 2012 and 2017. Many of the chosen names honor Soviet intelligence officers, military commanders, and officials connected to the Soviet seizure of the islands in 1945. Those commemorated include Pavel Fitin, who led Soviet foreign intelligence from 1939 to 1946; General Kuzma Derevyanko, who signed Japan’s Instrument of Surrender for the Soviet Union aboard the USS Missouri; and General Alexei Gnechko, who commanded the Soviet operation that seized the Kurils in 1945.
Japan has consistently protested Russian symbolic activities on the disputed islands. Tokyo considers Russia’s control of the Southern Kurils an illegal occupation, as the Soviet Union seized the islands in 1945 while the Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact remained intact. Japan renounced its claim to the Kuril Islands under the 1951 San Francisco Peace Treaty, but Tokyo claims the disputed islands are not part of the Kuril group.
Russia rejects Japan’s interpretation and maintains that its sovereignty over the islands is not open for discussion.

articles.title: Germany’s Deportation of an Afghan Without Criminal Record Sets a New Precedent
articles.full_text:
Germany stepped up its deportations of Afghan nationals even as critics take aim at its interactions with the Taliban regime.
In August 2024, Germany became the first European country to deport Afghan nationals to Afghanistan since the Taliban’s takeover. The deportation process was facilitated by Qatar. This happened after Germany’s “Traffic Light Coalition” government decided to change the rules to deport foreign nationals found guilty of serious crimes, a policy shift motivated by a deadly knife attack on a police officer in Mannheim.
At the time, Germany’s then-Chancellor Olaf Scholz said that Germany would not tolerate religious extremists or criminals who exploit the country’s laws protecting refugees. He added, “Such criminals should be deported even if they come from Syria and Afghanistan. Serious criminals and terrorists have no place here. In such cases the security interests of Germany outweigh the perpetrator’s interests in protection.” 
Last week, Germany deported an Afghan national without a criminal record for the first time since the Taliban’s return to power in 2021. The Afghan national had attempted to settle in another European country but was found to be illegally living there. He was transferred back to Germany and deported to Afghanistan by plane with 30 other deportees; all of the other deportees had criminal convictions. 
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that the man had become eligible for deportation after his ⁠asylum claim was denied. The minister told journalists, according to Deutsche Welle’s summary, that “anyone who has gone through an asylum process resulting in a rejection is therefore required to leave the country and must expect deportation if they do not depart voluntarily.” He called it a “shift in migration policy” marked by “control, a clear course, and a firm stance.” However, the deportation of an Afghan national without a criminal record sparked strong opposition from human rights groups.
When the deportation occurred, around 260 people attended a protest at the airport’s departure gate. Luca Müller, the spokesperson for the group behind the demonstration, argued that Germany’s government was “supporting the Islamist Taliban through its deals.” Both the political opposition and human rights organizations have accused the German government of legitimizing the de facto Taliban rule in Afghanistan in the name of facilitating deportations.
Responding to similar accusations in Germany’s Parliament from The Greens, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz rejected criticism that Germany’s engagement with the Taliban amounts to normalizing relations with them. He said that “any cooperation is limited to technical matters and serves Germany’s national interests.” He further stressed that “we are not normalizing this regime.” 
However, Merz also highlighted that “diplomatic relations exist between states, not between governments. And there have always been diplomatic relations with Afghanistan.”
In July 2025, the German government announced that it had permitted two Taliban envoys to enter Germany in order to facilitate the deportation of Afghan nationals with criminal records. This was the first time that Taliban officials were allowed to enter any major Western country since the group’s forceful takeover of Kabul in August 2021. A year after the Taliban officials’ arrival in Germany, the group’s representatives now head both the Afghan Consulate General in Bonn and the Afghan embassy in Berlin, where four new Taliban envoys arrived this year, bringing the total number to six.
After Germany’s move to engage directly with the Taliban, the European Union followed suit. In October 2025, the EU confirmed that it was engaging with the de facto regime in Kabul as part of its efforts to increase deportations of failed asylum seekers from Europe. Markus Lammert, a spokesman for the EU’s executive, said at the time that the European Commission had “initiated exploratory contacts at the technical level with the de facto authorities in Afghanistan.” 
The move came after a majority of the EU member states urged Brussels to reach out to the Taliban in Afghanistan. In a letter initiated by Belgium, 20 EU member states called on the European Commission to take action in order to enable both voluntary and involuntary deportation of Afghans with no legal right to stay in Europe. As per EU data, the member states of the Union received about 1 million asylum applications from Afghan nationals between 2013 and 2024, out of which about half have been approved.
Following last year’s initial contact with the Taliban, in June 2026, the EU hosted Taliban officials for the highest-level contacts between the two since the summer of 2021. The Belgian government granted the Taliban officials one-day visas for talks on the deportation of Afghans whose asylum applications were rejected within the member states of the Union. 
The European Commission confirmed that the exchange between the Taliban delegation and the bloc’s member states was held at a technical level and focused on the deportation of Afghan nationals to Afghanistan. The Commission also confirmed that representatives from 15, out of a total 27, member states participated in the talks. 
Abdul Qahar Balkhi, who led the Taliban’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs delegation, said that both sides talked about “restarting broad-range consular services for Afghans in [the] EU zone, including [the] need for trust-building measures, consular presence and dignified return process.”
Like the developments in Germany, the EU’s move has also been criticized by human rights groups. Amnesty International urged the EU and member states to withdraw their Afghanistan deportation plans and put an end to any cooperation with the Taliban. Amnesty further highlighted that Afghanistan cannot be considered safe for return, and that deportation of Afghans would put their lives at risk. Eve Geddie, director of Amnesty International’s European Institutions Office, said that “any EU engagement on deportations to Afghanistan is reckless, dangerous, and ignores the EU’s own legal obligations.”
Since the Taliban’s takeover, deportation has remained a controversial topic due to concerns about human rights and the treatment of returnees. Nevertheless, Germany has returned over 200 people to Afghanistan since 2024. Amnesty International reported that at least one has been killed following deportation. 
The deportation of an Afghan national without any criminal record sets a new precedent for Germany. That raises serious concerns among the almost 450,000 individuals of Afghan origin who currently live in Germany, many of whom arrived as refugees.

articles.title: How Aging Populations Are Transforming Police Work Across Asia
articles.full_text:
In East Asia’s graying societies, police are becoming the “catch-all” agency for managing aging, like dementia-related wandering.
About one-third of East Asia’s population is projected to be 60 or older by 2050, making it the world’s fastest-aging region. Public debates about population aging have largely centered on its effects on democratic governance, economic growth, pension sustainability, healthcare, urban planning, and housing policy. Yet one area remains notably underdiscussed: policing. 
Across graying societies, police are becoming the “catch-all” agency for managing aging as their roles and workloads have expanded in unprecedented ways. Police officers frequently mobilize to search for missing seniors and answer late-night calls from those who are confused or disoriented. As AI-powered scams become increasingly common, officers are playing a growing role as educators and protectors, helping older adults recognize and avoid financial fraud. They are often the first on the scene when older adults experience falls, heart attacks, strokes, or other medical emergencies. They are also on the front lines of social service delivery, responding to mounting cases of elder abuse or neglect and routinely conducting welfare checks as social isolation and kinship erosion damage mental health. Furthermore, increasing traffic incidents involving elderly drivers have prompted the police to engage in driver safety campaigns and to identify and report at-risk older drivers. 
Beneath this expanding portfolio of aging-related police work lies a revolution in policing and governance more broadly. Silver policing in East Asia is fostering greater intersectoral coordination and shifting the role of the police to that of a facilitator within a broader network. This reflects mounting pressure in East Asian governance to decentralize solutions and incorporate more horizontal partnerships among diverse actors, moving away from historically favored top-down solutions to pressing policy challenges.  
Dementia-related wandering brings this emerging reality into sharper focus. With 57 million people living with dementia worldwide and the total expected to nearly triple to 152 million by 2050, responding to wandering has emerged as a critical policing function. The lion’s share of the world’s dementia patients reside in the Asia-Pacific region, with some studies predicting that nearly half of all dementia patients will live there by mid-century. Studies show that between 27 percent and 70 percent of community-dwelling people with dementia go missing, and significant police resources are allocated to search and rescue. Wandering can be fatal, and search efforts are time-sensitive; in some studies, up to half of people with dementia who go missing and are not found within 24 hours end up seriously injured or dead. 
The surging demands on the police require establishing new partnerships rather than fine-tuning traditional, centralized, hierarchical organizational structures and procedures. Police must now work rapidly and closely with hospitals, clinics, and long-term care facilities to determine whether a missing person has been admitted or located. Neighborhood associations, resident groups, and trained volunteers support search efforts, while families and caregivers strengthen prevention by registering older adults with dementia in local alert systems and equipping them with GPS tracking devices. Transit operators, retailers, and other businesses also serve as important community partners by staying alert for wandering older adults and reporting potential sightings. 
As coordination among police and other societal actors has intensified, countries have adapted and leveraged their existing infrastructure to scale these emerging collaborative solutions. Rather than building entirely new systems, each country has repurposed its existing strengths – such as transportation networks, urban planning, education systems, digital infrastructure, surveillance technologies, or biometric identification platforms – as the backbone for cross-sector collaboration that enables police to extend their capacity. Thus, a common thread across East Asia is not institutional convergence but infrastructural adaptation.
Singapore, for example, addresses dementia-related wandering by capitalizing on its world-leading urban infrastructure to expand police search capacity. It has over 800 “Dementia Go-To Points” located in public transit stations, supermarkets, and eldercare centers, where community members can bring seemingly lost persons for assistance from trained staff. Many older adults carry QR codes that link to their caretakers’ contact information, helping transform the city into a dementia-supportive network that extends the reach of the police.
Japan mobilizes its educational infrastructure to strengthen its community guardianship model – built around neighborhood police stations (koban), social workers, businesses, volunteers, and residents who assist in searches for dementia wanderers through their “SOS networks.” Thousands of these networks are found throughout the country, from megacities such as Tokyo to smaller cities like Omuta, and require high public awareness. Accordingly, children are taught in schools and through community-based education about dementia and how to respond to wandering seniors, forming a plexus of intergenerational support within the local community. The entire community serves as a safety net to prevent older adults with dementia from going missing or being seriously hurt, and an educated community becomes a standing alert and active care system that the police can mobilize. 
The Hong Kong Police Force, in contrast, takes advantage of the city’s extensive transportation infrastructure to create a large-scale, coordinated observation and interception system for locating missing older adults. Unlike in automobile-dependent societies, wandering older adults in Hong Kong are likely to use the city’s extensive Mass Transit Railway (MTR), one of the world’s busiest and most heavily used, operating more than 7,500 rail services and carrying over 4.7 million riders daily. In an unprecedented partnership with MTR, the police can enter the missing older adult’s identity-linked transit card number (called the Octopus, which is possessed by 98 percent of the working-age population) into the MTR system so that its use automatically alerts station staff and notifies the police of the individual’s location, while preventing the card from functioning at exit gates and directing the person to station staff for assistance.
China leverages its extensive surveillance infrastructure alongside an auxiliary online crowdsourcing platform to scale coordination. The police rely on integrated command platforms that enable them and other municipal agencies to access and coordinate information from CCTV networks. Over 700 million cameras in China are estimated to be in operation, roughly one camera for every two people. Moreover, ubiquitous drones help pinpoint a person’s location to aid the on-the-ground search. China also mobilizes millions of smartphone users through crowdsourcing apps such as Douyin Xunren (a public-interest missing-person service), creating a hybrid search architecture that combines state coordination with citizen participation to support police efforts. 
South Korea and Taiwan have integrated police work with tracking and identification infrastructure to collectively prevent wandering in the first place. The South Korean police, health agencies, and local governments have distributed GPS devices directly to people with dementia, at dementia safety centers, and through biometric identification of registered dementia patients. Families pre-register dementia patients’ guardians’ contact information, fingerprints, and photos in a centralized police database, enabling faster identification and reunification if the person is later found disoriented. Similarly, in Taiwan, biometric pre-registration, especially fingerprinting, combined with ID bracelets and other tracking devices (in some cities, a low-power Bluetooth positioning device that looks like a lucky charm from local temples is given to the elderly to increase adoption), enables rapid identification and reunification. 
As the harbinger of silver policing, East Asia offers a glimpse into the future of other countries. By 2030, one in six people worldwide will be 60 or older, and issues such as dementia-related wandering will become more prevalent. East Asia teaches us that meeting these demographic challenges will require new forms of governance, even in policy spheres like public security, where governments have zealously guarded their authority to dictate solutions to citizens. 
Traditional roles are breaking down and evolving. Police work is no longer defined solely by responding to crime but increasingly by safeguarding vulnerable populations. Policymakers will need to promote polycentric solutions by adapting each country’s existing infrastructure to scale multisector collaboration. Yes, this will break down institutional boundaries, redistribute responsibility across public, private, and community actors, and transform how governments, including the police, function, but this may be the only way to meet growing needs in aging societies.
