articles.title: Is Japan Decoupling From China?
articles.full_text:
The new generation of Japanese policymakers is far less willing to accommodate China than its predecessors.
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae (left) shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Gyeongju, South Korea, Oct. 31, 2025.
Japan’s relationship with the People’s Republic of China (PRC) began before formal diplomatic relations were established. Although diplomatic relations were not normalized until 1972, the two countries had already created an unofficial trade mechanism in 1962 that enabled bilateral trade despite the absence of mutual diplomatic recognition.
In a famous article published in Foreign Affairs in 1967, former U.S. Vice President Richard Nixon argued that “we simply cannot afford to leave China forever outside the family of nations.” At the time, Japan’s China policy had already been moving in that direction, going beyond even the policy imagination of its closest ally, the United States.
This was despite intense diplomatic pressure from the United States, which remained firmly anti-communist. Throughout the 1960s, Washington publicly opposed Japan’s efforts to normalize relations with one of its closest neighbors and discouraged any move toward diplomatic recognition of the PRC. The “shock” caused by Nixon’s announcement of his planned visit to mainland China in 1971 stemmed, in part, from Japanese frustration that this policy framework toward China – shaped and constrained by U.S. diplomatic pressure against Japan’s preference – was abruptly reversed without prior consultation with Tokyo.
After normalization, Japan and China entered a honeymoon period in which their relationship resembled a quasi-alliance, rooted in their shared distrust of the Soviet Union as a common adversary. This perception was also shared by the United States, which intensified its pressure against Moscow as Cold War tensions began to rise. From the late 1970s through the 1980s, Japan expanded its industrial assistance to China, while the United States strengthened military cooperation with Beijing, including transfers of military technology. These developments highlight the strategic importance that both Japan and the United States placed on their relationship with China.
A turning point in China-Japan relations came on June 4, 1989, when the People’s Liberation Army moved into Tiananmen Square to suppress student protesters. Images of the violence were broadcast around the world, prompting the U.S.-led Western bloc to impose sanctions in response to China’s violent crackdown. 
Although Japan suspended its aid program to China, it was reluctant to fully participate in broader sanctions. It was Japan, at the critical G7 summit in Paris, that took the lead in preventing China’s complete isolation from the international community. Its efforts resulted in the inclusion of the following sentence in the summit declaration: “We look to the Chinese authorities to create conditions which will avoid their isolation and provide for a return to cooperation based upon the resumption of movement towards political and economic reform, and openness.” At that critical juncture, Japan was prepared to break with the emerging Western consensus in order to prevent China from being pushed back into international isolation.
The history reviewed above is essential for understanding the current state of China-Japan relations. Since the 1960s, the two nations have consistently maintained some level of economic exchange despite the political circumstances of each period. The characterization of their relationship as “hot economics and cold politics” has been a defining feature of bilateral ties, particularly over the past several decades. During the 1980s, and especially in the aftermath of the Tiananmen Incident, a strategic dimension also helped sustain the partnership, as both countries continued to view their relationship through the lens of shared geopolitical interests.
However, when examining the China-Japan relationship today, it may be more accurately described as one of “cooling economics and colder politics” – a trajectory that relations had not previously taken.
The turn of events can be traced back to Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s controversial statements in late 2025 hinting at the possible deployment of Japan’s Self-Defense Forces in the event of a crisis surrounding Taiwan. Some have argued that Takaichi’s remarks were bold and resolute, while others have criticized them as insensitive to China’s red lines and emblematic of her tendency toward gaffes. Regardless of the interpretation, what is clear is that Beijing was provoked by Takaichi’s statements and has sought to apply maximum pressure on Japan in response.
Even after Takaichi’s electoral victory in early 2026, China has continued to exert pressure on critical mineral supply chains and impose targeted export controls not only on Japanese defense firms but also on companies involved in dual-use technologies. The effects of China’s export controls on rare earths – a sector in which China possesses nearly 90 percent of global refining capacity – have already been felt by Japanese companies. Furthermore, the arrest of Japanese company employees in mainland China on allegations of illegally exporting rare earth magnets has further unsettled Japanese businesses that remain heavily reliant on the Chinese market. 
At the same time, diplomatic relations remain stagnant, with a bilateral summit between Xi Jinping and Takaichi appearing unlikely in the near future.
While Japan remains open to a reset in its relationship with China, it appears to be gradually but decisively preparing for a future with reduced dependence on Beijing, reversing a decades-long trend of courting and nurturing its neighbor. This shift was represented in Takaichi’s “updated free and open Indo-Pacific” speech, in which she upheld the core principles inherited from her predecessors while also highlighting the importance of economic security and resilient supply chains with like-minded nations. 
Although the country driving this necessity was not explicitly named, China’s ongoing economic pressure makes it difficult not to identify Beijing as the force behind this policy shift. This development may ultimately place limits on how broadly Japan’s strategic concept of a “free and open” Indo-Pacific can continue to accommodate China. However, at present, Japan appears to prioritize responding to geopolitical realities rather than attempting to sugarcoat them.
One theory explaining Japan’s shift in its approach toward China is generational change. The old China hands in Japan held a special sentiment toward mainland China. They were deeply aware that their generation, as well as that of their parents, had been connected to a period in which Japan inflicted immense suffering and destruction across China, as the Empire of Japan fully mobilized its military power from the late 1930s until the end of World War II. While they viewed investment in China as a commercial opportunity, they also regarded it as a means of addressing the wrongs committed by their nation and expressing gratitude for the PRC government’s decision to forgo war reparations. 
However, the China hands who once held influential positions within the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) are now aging and gradually exiting the political scene. They are being replaced by a younger generation of more hawkish conservatives who seek to hedge against China and deepen ties with Taiwan. It is striking that both Takaichi and Ishiba Shigeru visited Taiwan before becoming prime ministers – as if doing so had become a rite of passage for aspiring Japanese political leaders.
The reason why younger generations of politicians do not share the same perception of China as their predecessors may be attributed, in part, to their understanding of history. From their perspective, the historical debt has already been repaid, and their generation should not be expected to bear responsibility for the wrongdoings of the past, which occurred before they were born. The statements of prominent conservative politicians such as former Prime Minister Abe Shinzo and Takaichi are emblematic of this changing understanding of history. In a 2015 official government statement, Abe declared that “we must not leave our children, grandchildren, and generations to come, who bear no responsibility for that war, with the obligation to continue apologizing indefinitely.” 
Similarly, back in 1994, the then up-and-coming Takaichi criticized Prime Minister Murayama Tomiichi, who would acknowledge and apologize for Japan’s wartime aggression against its neighbors the next year, arguing that “I do not think it is acceptable for someone to offer an apology on my behalf without my consent.” Whether this generational shift reflects a lack of historical awareness or a different interpretation of Japan’s wartime is unclear. Nevertheless, it is notable that both Abe and Takaichi have drawn particularly strong support from younger generations.
At certain points in history, Japan was among the few nations willing to engage with China despite international opposition, investing heavily without fully considering how such efforts might later be used against it. Today, with a fundamentally different relationship and balance of power between the two nations, Japan appears to be preparing for a new era. Today, the obligation to keep China integrated into the international community and maintain extensive economic ties regardless of the cost is no longer viewed as an imperative.

articles.title: Uzbekistan’s Nuclear Power Plant Project Advances
articles.full_text:
Officials say that the first small modular reactor of Uzbekistan’s nuclear power plant project is to be commissioned in 2029.
The head of Uzatom, Uzbekistan’s atomic energy agency, Azim Akhmedkhadjayev said recently that the first small modular reactor of Uzbekistan’s ongoing nuclear power plant (NPP) project is to be commissioned in 2029, while the first large reactor will come online in 2033. The project itself will be completed in 2034-2035. The NPP will produce up to 17 billion kWh of electricity per year, which, according to Akhmedkhadjayev, will amount to 20 percent of the country’s energy production. Current annual production volume is 80 billion kWh.
Having an NPP is not a new dream for Uzbekistan. The first president of the country, Islam Karimov, also understood the need for a nuclear power plant, but never took concrete steps toward its realization. Shavkat Mirziyoyev, however, did not waste any time. In December 2017, just a year after Mirziyoyev came to power, Tashkent and Rosatom, the Russian state nuclear energy corporation, agreed to build a two-reactor NPP in Uzbekistan. 
In 2019, Tashkent adopted a law “On the Use of Atomic Energy for Peaceful Purposes,” outlining a legal framework that includes state ownership rules, safety protocols, and so on. In 2024, Uzatom was established as an authorized body to implement state policy under the Cabinet of Ministers, replacing the Agency for the Development of Atomic Energy that had existed under the Ministry of Energy. 
After years of negotiation and consideration of several different options, in September 2025, Uzbekistan and Rosatom finally signed an agreement to build an integrated nuclear power plant in Jizzakh with two small modular reactors (SMRs), specifically RITM-200N reactors, with a capacity of 55 megawatts each, and two large VVER-1000 reactors, each generating 1 GW. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Uzbekistan’s Mirziyoyev officially launched the construction of the plant in June this year at a ceremony held in Saint Petersburg.
The project was initially estimated to cost $10-13 billion; however, last month, Uzatom’s Akhmadkhodjayev said that the expected cost is $9.5 billion at most. Even this figure is arguably too big for Uzbekistan, whose external debt is already over $82 billion as of early 2026. Tashkent plans to attract around 85-90 percent of the NPP construction funds in the form of loans from diverse sources, hoping it will return over $165 billion to the state budget. 
Tashkent has been trying to present the project as multilaterally financed; a project free from Russian loans. 
“We are not currently considering Russian money, given all the geopolitical developments,” said Akhmadkhodjayev in March 2025. At the time, the project under consideration consisted of six small modular reactors, which were estimated to have a price tag of just $2 billion. He argued that the construction of the plant would not place Uzbekistan in a debt trap despite most of the money being planned to be borrowed from external actors. 
“They [investors, lenders] will receive the profits generated by the nuclear power plant in the form of dividends. They will not have any involvement in the management [of the plant]. This is stupid,” explained Akhmadkhodjayev. 
Half a year later, after the project had been revised to its final form — consisting of two small modular reactors and two large capacity reactors — the head of the directorate for the construction of nuclear power plants in Uzbekistan, Abdujamil Qalmuratov, voiced a different cost: $1 billion for the small reactors. He said that the money will come from the state budget. 
“Yes, it’s the state budget. The state is building it — it’s a completely Uzbek project. The source of funding is our budget. The nuclear project must be national,” reinstated Qalmuratov.
Tashkent obviously prioritizes, at least in its rhetoric, its sovereignty and control of the NPP project.  But it has not closed doors in Moscow’s face. In June 2026, as the construction of the plant in Jizzakh began, Russian President Vladimir Putin signaled his readiness to make a financial commitment for the project, offering a preferential export loan. 
“It is important that Russia will not only build the nuclear power plant, but will also provide its Uzbek partners with a preferential export loan and provide support throughout the entire life cycle of the plant,” noted Putin. 
It is unlikely that Uzbekistan can cover the entire project with the state budget, so Tashkent is currently window shopping for external loans. Putin’s comment seems to be more of a political statement than a real deal, since no numbers have been given and there has been no news of a confirmed deal. Tashkent is likely exploring all of its options (including Chinese investment or multilateral financing through BRICS’ New Development Bank), trying to diversify the source of the funds so as not to tie itself to one actor, especially to Russia. 
Not only does Tashkent intend to avoid Russian money, it is also actively trying to avoid full reliance on Russia in the construction, supply, and operating process. Last year Uzatom stated that it would form an international consortium to carry out the NPP project, seeking to employ not only Russian technology but also Chinese non-nuclear technologies, as well as European soft and hardware products. The agency also repeatedly states that the project is “under the strict supervision” of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), signaling that the NPP is not an opaque, Moscow-controlled facility beyond outside scrutiny. 
Tashkent is afraid that Western sanctions might affect the project, as they seem to have affected the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant – another Rosatom flagship nuclear plant project in Turkiye. Rosatom’s Director General Dmitry Likhachev spoke in May about the impacts of sanctions on its ongoing nuclear projects. Tashkent is observing that situation in real time and clearly thinking of how to protect its own plans. Involving as many diverse partners and lenders as possible is arguably a gambit to avoid the fate of the Akkuyu project. 
Other questions arise when considering what will happen even after the plant is constructed. It has been promoted as necessary to fulfill Uzbekistan’s growing domestic energy demands. But, as the project requires an external loan that Tashkent will need to pay back, it is likely that much of the energy generated by the NPP will be sold to neighboring countries to make quick cash instead of meeting domestic demand. 
Uzbekistan, which used to import electricity just a decade ago, has already become an electricity exporter, with the majority of this export going to neighboring countries. In 2025, Uzbekistan exported 500 million kWh of electricity to Kazakhstan, 400 million kWh to Tajikistan, 1.2 billion kWh to Kyrgyzstan, and more than 2 billion kWh to Afghanistan – all while citizens of Uzbekistan keep experiencing power outages due to high demand in peak seasons such as mid-summer and mid-winder. This approach, which in the eyes of many Uzbeks appears to prioritize the needs of its neighbors, is most likely linked to water-energy diplomacy (with Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, as they are upper-stream countries along the region’s two major rivers) and energy-support diplomacy (with Afghanistan). But people will become less patient with electricity shortages once the NPP starts operating, and that presents a genuine challenge for Tashkent.
The head of Uzatom, Uzbekistan’s atomic energy agency, Azim Akhmedkhadjayev said recently that the first small modular reactor of Uzbekistan’s ongoing nuclear power plant (NPP) project is to be commissioned in 2029, while the first large reactor will come online in 2033. The project itself will be completed in 2034-2035. The NPP will produce up to 17 billion kWh of electricity per year, which, according to Akhmedkhadjayev, will amount to 20 percent of the country’s energy production. Current annual production volume is 80 billion kWh.
Having an NPP is not a new dream for Uzbekistan. The first president of the country, Islam Karimov, also understood the need for a nuclear power plant, but never took concrete steps toward its realization. Shavkat Mirziyoyev, however, did not waste any time. In December 2017, just a year after Mirziyoyev came to power, Tashkent and Rosatom, the Russian state nuclear energy corporation, agreed to build a two-reactor NPP in Uzbekistan. 
In 2019, Tashkent adopted a law “On the Use of Atomic Energy for Peaceful Purposes,” outlining a legal framework that includes state ownership rules, safety protocols, and so on. In 2024, Uzatom was established as an authorized body to implement state policy under the Cabinet of Ministers, replacing the Agency for the Development of Atomic Energy that had existed under the Ministry of Energy. 
After years of negotiation and consideration of several different options, in September 2025, Uzbekistan and Rosatom finally signed an agreement to build an integrated nuclear power plant in Jizzakh with two small modular reactors (SMRs), specifically RITM-200N reactors, with a capacity of 55 megawatts each, and two large VVER-1000 reactors, each generating 1 GW. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Uzbekistan’s Mirziyoyev officially launched the construction of the plant in June this year at a ceremony held in Saint Petersburg.
The project was initially estimated to cost $10-13 billion; however, last month, Uzatom’s Akhmadkhodjayev said that the expected cost is $9.5 billion at most. Even this figure is arguably too big for Uzbekistan, whose external debt is already over $82 billion as of early 2026. Tashkent plans to attract around 85-90 percent of the NPP construction funds in the form of loans from diverse sources, hoping it will return over $165 billion to the state budget. 
Tashkent has been trying to present the project as multilaterally financed; a project free from Russian loans. 
“We are not currently considering Russian money, given all the geopolitical developments,” said Akhmadkhodjayev in March 2025. At the time, the project under consideration consisted of six small modular reactors, which were estimated to have a price tag of just $2 billion. He argued that the construction of the plant would not place Uzbekistan in a debt trap despite most of the money being planned to be borrowed from external actors. 
“They [investors, lenders] will receive the profits generated by the nuclear power plant in the form of dividends. They will not have any involvement in the management [of the plant]. This is stupid,” explained Akhmadkhodjayev. 
Half a year later, after the project had been revised to its final form — consisting of two small modular reactors and two large capacity reactors — the head of the directorate for the construction of nuclear power plants in Uzbekistan, Abdujamil Qalmuratov, voiced a different cost: $1 billion for the small reactors. He said that the money will come from the state budget. 
“Yes, it’s the state budget. The state is building it — it’s a completely Uzbek project. The source of funding is our budget. The nuclear project must be national,” reinstated Qalmuratov.
Tashkent obviously prioritizes, at least in its rhetoric, its sovereignty and control of the NPP project.  But it has not closed doors in Moscow’s face. In June 2026, as the construction of the plant in Jizzakh began, Russian President Vladimir Putin signaled his readiness to make a financial commitment for the project, offering a preferential export loan. 
“It is important that Russia will not only build the nuclear power plant, but will also provide its Uzbek partners with a preferential export loan and provide support throughout the entire life cycle of the plant,” noted Putin.
articles.summary: Officials say that the first small modular reactor of Uzbekistan’s nuclear power plant project is to be commissioned in 2029.

articles.title: Pakistan Wields Iron Fist Against Protesters in Pakistan-administered Jammu and Kashmir
articles.full_text:
Last week, Pakistani Defense Minister Khwaja Asif described protesters “as enemies like India.”
Screenshot of a JKJAAC video showing protesters in Pakistan-administered Jammu and Kashmir on a “Long March,” August 2, 2026.
At least 21 protesters were killed and dozens of others injured when Pakistani security forces opened fire on protesters in Pakistan-administered Jammu and Kashmir (PaJK) on July 27. The protesters, who were led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a grass roots grouping of traders, students and civil society organizations in PaJK, had gathered at Rawalakot and began marching toward Muzaffarabad, PaJK’s capital, when the crackdown began.
Casualty figures are contested and hard to confirm as the Pakistan government has imposed a blanket shutdown on communications across PaJK.
When the Pakistani government proscribed JAAC under anti-terrorism legislation on June 5, PaJK erupted in protest. An estimated 40 people, including six police and paramilitary personnel, are reported to have been killed between June 5 and July 24.
Formed in 2023, JAAC initially mobilized on the issue of rising wheat and electricity prices. Since last year, its demands have taken on a decidedly political hue, with demonstrations now focusing on governance, electoral reforms, and constitutional issues.
Pakistan has long projected PaJK as a self-governing territory; indeed, the official name of PaJK is Azad (or free) Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) and its chief executive goes by the title of prime minister. However, the reality is that substantive powers and decision-making authority rest with Islamabad. AJK’s independence or even autonomy is a “myth.”
JAAC appears to be seeking to wrest back that authority by challenging political structures.
Foremost among its demands is the abolition of “refugee seats” in the PaJK legislative assembly, which are reserved for descendants of those who migrated from Indian Kashmir after 1947, most of whom do not actually live in PaJK.
Of the PaJK legislature’s 53 seats, 12 are reserved for refugees, eight for women, ulema (Islamic scholars) and technocrats, leaving 33 for direct election. While the refugee seats can be defended on the grounds that they provide representation for the displaced, their structure is undemocratic. As political analyst Luv Puri told me in a recent interview, “refugee constituencies [wield] greater electoral influence per voter” than non-refugee constituencies in PaJK. Moreover, in effect the refugee seats have served to enhance Islamabad’s capacity to significantly influence government formation and manipulate decisions in the PaJK assembly.
Indeed, every Pakistani political party has manipulated the refugee seats to form the PaJK government. In the 2021 election, just two PaJK parties won a seat each.
The current surge in unrest in PaJK comes amid elections to its legislative assembly, which began on July 27 and will end on August 10.
The protests in PaJK have grown in magnitude over the past two months and their geographic spread has expanded as well. Rawalakot was the epicenter of the protests until last week, but unrest has now spilled over to Muzaffarabad, Mirpur and other districts. The lethality of the Pakistani government’s response to the protests has grown too.
The mounting casualties could transform the mass protests into a political movement.
Of course, the Pakistani government can be expected to unleash the full force of their iron fist before the movement morphs into something bigger.
Brute force has always been the response of Pakistan’s establishment to protests and resistance. Moreover, this crisis is unfolding in PaJK.
Pakistani leaders often refer to Kashmir as Pakistan’s jugular vein, which cannot be severed from Pakistan. Indeed, Kashmir is the one issue on which Pakistanis stand united.
Having spent billions of dollars and much diplomatic capital on failing to wrest away control over Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir (IaJK), Islamabad cannot afford to allow PaJK to slip out of its control, however minimally, under any circumstances.
“While Islamabad did negotiate with the JAAC, its commitment to finding a political solution was less than half-hearted,” a Mirpuri based in the United Kingdom told The Diplomat on condition of anonymity. Even as it engaged in talks, it was “increasing deployment of paramilitary personnel in PaJK to crush what is a political movement.” Its designation of the PaJK as terrorist, and “the arrest of hundreds of political activists in midnight raids, are aimed at provoking the local residents to turn to violence.” That would in turn serve to justify Islamabad’s use of extreme force against the people of PaJK, she said.
Amid its deadly crackdown on protesters last week, Pakistani Defense Minister Khwaja Asif said: “I put the protesters of Azad Kashmir in the same category as India and consider them also as enemies like India.”
His comment does not bode well for the people of PaJK. By portraying the protesters as “enemies,” Asif is preparing to deploy the iron fist on PaJK.
At a time when Pakistan is grappling with economic crises, and powerful armed insurgencies in Balochistan and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, Islamabad could use the crisis in PaJK to unite a divided Pakistan.

articles.title: Is Islamic Extremism Taking Over Bangladesh?
articles.full_text:
Two years after Sheikh Hasina’s ouster, what is the role of Islamist movements in Bangladesh?
Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Shafiqur Rahman addresses an election rally in Chattogram district, Bangladesh, Feb. 2, 2026.
For 15 years, Bangladesh’s government was viewed as a firm bulwark against religious extremism. Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina had cracked down heavily on the country’s largest Islamist party, Jamaat-e-Islami, as well as various radical and jihadist outfits. 
Really, Hasina cracked down on everyone – but to some, her authoritarian bent was an acceptable price to pay to keep religious extremism under wraps.
So when Hasina’s Awami League government was ousted from power on August 5, 2024, it triggered a wave of deep anxiety. Many feared that Islamists in Bangladesh would now have free rein. India, especially, was horrified by the prospect of its eastern neighbor becoming a safe haven for Islamist extremist groups – some of which might dream of carrying out terrorist attacks on Indian soil.
Now, two years after the collapse of Hasina’s government, Jamaat-e-Islami has made a spectacular return to parliamentary politics. Radical groups are mobilizing, and there are escalating attacks against religious minorities. 
Does that mean fears about Bangladesh’s Islamist explosion have come true? Not exactly.

articles.title: 12 Asian Countries Subject to Finalized US Visa Bond Program
articles.full_text:
The program, which launched as a pilot in August 2025, is now permanent and at present affects the citizens of 50 countries.
The United States State Department has made permanent its pilot visa bond program, under which citizens of listed foreign countries seeking to obtain business or tourism visas to come to the United States may be required to pay a significant sum – a bond of up to $20,000 – to obtain a visa.
As stated in the Federal Register notice, the program will be limited to those who are applying for business visitor/tourist (B-1/B-2) nonimmigrant visas and are citizens of specific countries identified by the State Department as “failing to meet rigorous standards relating to overstays, information sharing, screening and vetting, civil, criminal and identity records, and document security.”
Among the 50 countries currently listed in the program, 12 are in Asia: Bangladesh, Cambodia, Fiji, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Nepal, Papua New Guinea, Tajikistan, Tonga, Turkmenistan, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu. The State Department explicitly framed the bond as ensuring that the visa-holder will maintain their nonimmigrant status – meaning they will not apply for asylum or refugee status – and that the individual will depart as required by the limits of their visa. 
The latest relevant notice, to be published in the Federal Register on August 3, claimed that the pilot program “has provided sufficient data to suggest that a visa bond program is an effective tool for enforcing compliance among bonded visa holders.” 
In FY 2024, the notice stated, there were 45,488 overstays from the 50 countries currently listed for the program. In the first 10 months of the pilot, it continued, “the number of overstays was fewer than 50.” Notably, the rates of visa issuances also dropped dramatically, falling by 83 percent compared to the same 10-month period in the prior year. Nearly half of the 20,000 applicants during the pilot period who were mandated to pay bonds in order to secure their visa decided not to. The notice put it like this: “some applicants appear to self-select by not paying a bond.” (Note: That “self-select” is perhaps better read as “self-reject.”)
The State Department understood this decline in overstay rates as the direct result of the bond program. There are, however, other ways to interpret these points of data. Dramatically fewer visas means dramatically fewer overstays.
The American reputation is not all that welcoming these days. According to data from the National Travel and Tourism Office and reporting by CNN, 4 million fewer foreign visitors visited the United States in 2025 compared to 2024. 2025 represented the worst single-year decline in tourism travel to the U.S. in two decades, excluding the 2020 pandemic. People, simply put, are less interested in traveling to the United States. The Trump administration’s widespread crackdown on immigration – of all kinds – has resulted in violence, including the killing of U.S. and foreign citizens by immigration agents.
For those foreigners who still want to visit the United States for tourism or business, the bond program adds yet another hurdle to an already arduous and, in some cases, expensive process. Non-petition-based nonimmigrant visas require a nonrefundable fee of $185, paid when submitting an application and scheduling an interview appointment. During the interview, for citizens of the listed countries, the consular officer decides whether a visa bond will be required – either $10,000, $15,000, or $20,000. The visa will then be denied. The denial can be overcome if the bond is paid; otherwise it stands as denial. The bond can be posted by the applicant or a third party, such as a friend, family member, or business associate. Once the bond is paid, the application will be reviewed again – the consular officer can decide to approve or deny the visa. If the visa is denied, the bond will be canceled; if it is approved, the bond becomes returnable once the visa expires and if the individual is no longer still in the United States.
Of the 12 Asian countries currently listed, three are in Central Asia (Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan), one is in East Asia (Mongolia), two are in South Asia (Bangladesh and Nepal), two are in Southeast Asia (Cambodia and Papua New Guinea), and four are in Oceania (Fiji, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu). 
As I’ve covered previously, the Trump administration’s hyperfocus on overstay rates – that is, the percentage rather than the actual number – draws a target on countries from which relatively few people travel to the U.S. at all. If the goal of the program is reduce the actual number of overstays, Tuvalu may not be country to punish. 
I’ve written previously in depth about Turkmenistan, which does have a relatively high overstay rate – 15.89 percent in 2024 for B-1/B-02 visa holders – and the reasons this measure is deceptive. That 15.89 percent figure represents just 320 people. Tajikistan’s overstay rate in 2024 was 7.57 percent, or 140 individual overstays. Kyrgyzstan’s overstay rate was lower than Turkmenistan’s, at 8.39 percent, but because of the higher number of travelers from Kyrgyzstan represented 643 people. 
For other countries, the listing makes even less sense – the numbers are even lower.
Tuvalu had an overstay rate of 11.63 percent in 2024 for B-1/B-02 visa holders. Out of 43 expected departures, five people overstayed their visas. Vanuatu had an overstay rate of 3.05 percent – hardly high – representing only five people as well. Fiji’s overstay rate in 2024 for business and tourism visas was just under 4 percent, or 294 overstays. Tonga’s rate was twice that of Fiji’s – 6.45 percent – but that figure represents just 152 overstays.
Bangladesh’s overstay rate in 2024 was 5.73 percent, representing more than 2,200 overstays. While Nepal saw just over 1,000 overstays in 2024, its rate was just 3.12 percent. And Bhutan? While it had one of the highest overstay rates in the entire world – 21.75 percent – this represented just 92 individual overstays. 
Furthermore, the reality is that even the lowest current end of the visa bond – $10,000 – represents an almost impossible sum for many people. The average gross monthly salary in Turkmenistan, according to wage.is, is estimated at around $714. In Tuvalu it’s $551. In Bangladesh, that figure is just $149.

articles.title: Myanmar’s Depleted Oil Pipeline
articles.full_text:
A cross-border energy project deals with the impact of two conflicts.
A sub-pumping station of Sino-Myanmar oil and gas pipelines in Longling County, Yunnan Province, China.
An oil pipeline carrying imported crude from Myanmar to China is facing a two-front crisis: armed conflict at home and a maritime blockade overseas.
The pipeline is connected to a crude oil terminal built to accommodate large tankers transporting fuel from the Middle East.  Earlier this year, artillery shells and other munitions reportedly landed in the port town of Kyaukphyu, a few miles from the pipeline and fuel storage tanks.
The Myanmar military’s frequent clashes with the Arakan Army, an insurgent group that now controls 90 percent of Rakhine State, pose a threat to China-funded energy projects in the region.
A slowdown in tanker traffic from the Persian Gulf has further dented the pipeline’s capacity to supply oil to China’s western provinces.
The maritime data firm Kpler reports that China’s oil imports, including deliveries from the Myanmar pipeline, were expected to fall to 6.78 million barrels per day for May, the “lowest level in almost a decade.”
Myanmar’s military currently controls only three coastal towns in Rakhine State. The Arakan Army (AA) won pivotal victories in December 2024, when its troops captured the military’s western command headquarters and took control of the 270-kilometer border with Bangladesh. “AA has emerged as the most powerful and influential rebel group in Myanmar’s decades-long civil war,” wrote a Dhaka-based academic in Jamestown, a defense policy publication in Washington, D.C.
The Arakan Army’s rapid consolidation of territory has “generated unease” in Beijing about the security of China-Myanmar projects in Rakhine State. In February, a power plant connected to the Kyaukphyu Special Economic Zone (SEZ) was dismantled for relocation.  “They are taking the plant apart as quickly as they can to avoid it getting damaged in the fighting,” a resident of Kyaukphyu township told Burma News International.  Clashes between the military and the AA took place three kilometers away from the project.
Myanmar’s State Administration Council passed a law in February 2025 permitting foreign private security firms to operate in the country. The legislation was reportedly passed to give China-affiliated ventures the option of reinforcing security arrangements at conflict-prone locations.
In June, Myanmar’s president was invited to Beijing for a state visit. Min Aung Hlaing was given a red-carpet welcome, but China’s President Xi Jinping hinted at the unrest in Rakhine State, urging the former army chief to “find a correct path of development that suits . . . national conditions.”
A joint statement glossed over the insurgency, focusing instead on “shared prosperity” through “timely implementation” of the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor. Three infrastructure projects were singled out as priority items: the Kyaukphyu Deep-Sea Port, the Muse-Mandalay Railway and the China-Myanmar oil and gas pipelines.
The Kyaukphyu SEZ, which includes the oil terminal and pipeline on Maday Island, is a dependable revenue source for the state-owned Myanma Oil and Gas Enterprise. Former deputy military chief Soe Win reportedly told a meeting of senior officials last March, “this project must succeed.” However, the June 2025 deadline for completion of the project has passed, and satellite photos show limited activity at the main site.
Beijing remains hopeful that some components of the SEZ can be salvaged. The Myanmar oil pipeline has reliably supplied crude to Yunnan Petrochemical, a state-owned energy enterprise near Kunming. The refinery manufactures petroleum products such as diesel and jet fuel for the domestic and Southeast Asian markets.
To protect its $1.2 billion investment in the energy project, China has pursued a “dual-track” approach, engaging with both the Myanmar military as well as the AA.  Beijing has come to terms with the AA’s control over Rakhine State and, in a “delicate balancing act,” attempts to restrain both sides from derailing China’s projects.
In an opinion piece for the Daily Star, Mohammad Sufiur Rahman, Dhaka’s former ambassador to Myanmar, wrote, “regardless of the political future of Rakhine State, it is likely that the Arakan Army and the Myanmar government will eventually reach an understanding on the completion of the project.” He added that Beijing “will seek to use its good offices” with both warring parties to protect its energy-related assets.
The Kyaukphyu SEZ was once a flagship Belt and Road project, designed to open China’s landlocked western states to a wider market. The oil pipeline, completed in 2014, was built as a “strategic hedge” against a potential disruption in the Strait of Malacca, the maritime artery that supplies 80 percent of China’s crude oil imports.
A decade later, Kyaukphyu’s Special Economic Zone has turned into a de facto war zone.

The pipeline is connected to a crude oil terminal built to accommodate large tankers transporting fuel from the Middle East.  Earlier this year, artillery shells and other munitions reportedly landed in the port town of Kyaukphyu, a few miles from the pipeline and fuel storage tanks.
The Myanmar military’s frequent clashes with the Arakan Army, an insurgent group that now controls 90 percent of Rakhine State, pose a threat to China-funded energy projects in the region.
A slowdown in tanker traffic from the Persian Gulf has further dented the pipeline’s capacity to supply oil to China’s western provinces.
The maritime data firm Kpler reports that China’s oil imports, including deliveries from the Myanmar pipeline, were expected to fall to 6.78 million barrels per day for May, the “lowest level in almost a decade.”
Myanmar’s military currently controls only three coastal towns in Rakhine State. The Arakan Army (AA) won pivotal victories in December 2024, when its troops captured the military’s western command headquarters and took control of the 270-kilometer border with Bangladesh. “AA has emerged as the most powerful and influential rebel group in Myanmar’s decades-long civil war,” wrote a Dhaka-based academic in Jamestown, a defense policy publication in Washington, D.C.
The Arakan Army’s rapid consolidation of territory has “generated unease” in Beijing about the security of China-Myanmar projects in Rakhine State. In February, a power plant connected to the Kyaukphyu Special Economic Zone (SEZ) was dismantled for relocation.  “They are taking the plant apart as quickly as they can to avoid it getting damaged in the fighting,” a resident of Kyaukphyu township told Burma News International.  Clashes between the military and the AA took place three kilometers away from the project.
Myanmar’s State Administration Council passed a law in February 2025 permitting foreign private security firms to operate in the country. The legislation was reportedly passed to give China-affiliated ventures the option of reinforcing security arrangements at conflict-prone locations.
In June, Myanmar’s president was invited to Beijing for a state visit. Min Aung Hlaing was given a red-carpet welcome, but China’s President Xi Jinping hinted at the unrest in Rakhine State, urging the former army chief to “find a correct path of development that suits . . . national conditions.”
A joint statement glossed over the insurgency, focusing instead on “shared prosperity” through “timely implementation” of the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor. Three infrastructure projects were singled out as priority items: the Kyaukphyu Deep-Sea Port, the Muse-Mandalay Railway and the China-Myanmar oil and gas pipelines.
The Kyaukphyu SEZ, which includes the oil terminal and pipeline on Maday Island, is a dependable revenue source for the state-owned Myanma Oil and Gas Enterprise. Former deputy military chief Soe Win reportedly told a meeting of senior officials last March, “this project must succeed.” However, the June 2025 deadline for completion of the project has passed, and satellite photos show limited activity at the main site.
Beijing remains hopeful that some components of the SEZ can be salvaged. The Myanmar oil pipeline has reliably supplied crude to Yunnan Petrochemical, a state-owned energy enterprise near Kunming. The refinery manufactures petroleum products such as diesel and jet fuel for the domestic and Southeast Asian markets.
articles.summary: A cross-border energy project deals with the impact of two conflicts.

articles.title: For a Gen Z Revolt, Pakistan Needs a Cause, Not a Captain
articles.full_text:
Imran Khan is undoubtedly popular. But building a protest movement that revolves around Khan and his freedom immediately excludes half the population.
Political activists of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaaf (PTI) participate in a street protest in Karachi, Pakistan, July 26, 2024.
The resignation of India’s Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan on July 25 was the first real concession Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government has made to street protesters in several years.
The protests were spearheaded by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online satirical initiative of Abhijeet Dipke. It was a response to a comment by Chief Justice Surya Kant, who described unemployed youth who “attack everyone” online as cockroaches. The CJP attracted a million sign-ups online and went on to draw youth to Jantar Mantar. But the movement it spurred was not about Dipke.
What galvanized the sit-in was the corruption that manifested in leaked question papers for the NEET medical exam, youth frustration over the sense of a rigged system, and joblessness. Police brutality, which India’s Gen Z put on display in reels and videos, catalyzed the mass rage with the Modi government.
These reels reached Karachi and Lahore within the hour. And then came the inevitable question: after Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nepal, and now India, where is Pakistan’s Gen Z revolt?
The question deserves to be taken seriously. Many may argue that the missing ingredient in Pakistan is anger, or nerve, or a leader whom young people can rally behind. Pakistan has all three in surplus.
What it lacks is a cause that unites Pakistanis across ethnic, political, and provincial lines.
Look at South Asia’s four recent Gen Z uprisings. Colombo in 2022 rose over empty fuel pumps and dark houses, and for the first time brought Sinhalese and Tamils, unions and students, the devout and the secular, into a single crowd. It had no leader and wanted none. Dhaka in 2024 began as a fight over a civil service job quota and, once the shooting started, coalesced into one powerful goal to oust Sheikh Hasina, which happened on August 4, 2024. Youth in Kathmandu burned their parliament building and media houses in September 2025 over corruption and a social media ban. They forced Prime Minister K P Sharma Oli out of power within two days.
Not one of these Gen Z revolts was a fan club. Not one was built around a politician. They were unified not by a blueprint for tomorrow, but by a breaking point with today.
Of the four Gen Z protests, Nepal’s was the most significant. That leaderless movement did not merely topple a government. Six months later it walked into an election and handed 182 of 275 seats to the Rastriya Swatantra Party, whose figurehead, the rapper-turned-Kathmandu mayor, Balen Shah, beat the once-powerful Oli in the latter’s stronghold. Frustration with the old guard that began in the street ended at the ballot box. It converted street power into a democratic win.
Pakistan has witnessed countless protests and agitations, some that even took on the country’s powerful military.
Indeed, in recent years, massive protests led by the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) have roiled Pakistan, but without success. This is because they are organized around an individual: Imran Khan. An immensely popular former captain of Pakistan’s cricket team, Khan formed the PTI and was Pakistan’s prime minister from August 2018 until April 2022
Khan rode to power with support from Pakistan’s all-powerful military, but fell afoul of the generals in late 2021. He was ousted from office through a parliamentary vote of no-confidence in April 2022.
Khan’s brief initial detention triggered widespread political unrest and then violent protests in May 2023. Violence targeting the military came in handy for the generals to crack down on Khan’s supporters. He was formally arrested and imprisoned in August 2023 and remains behind bars following convictions in multiple legal cases involving corruption and state secrets. Khan and his party contend that these charges are politically motivated to block his political comeback.
The PTI-led protests demanding that Khan be set free are built on an individual, and have been very different than the recent Gen Z protests built on shared grievance.
While a cause can build coalitions, a politician can be divisive. “The economy has collapsed” implicates a whole country and can hold together people who agree on nothing else. “Free Imran Khan,” in contrast, implicates one half of the country and repels the other.
That distinction is pertinent to the Pakistani context. Youth respond to every mobilization already sorted into camps: Youthia, Patwari, or Jiyala, which are slang terms for die-hard supporters of Imran Khan’s PTI, Nawaz Sharif’s PML-N, and Bilawal Bhutto’s PPP, respectively.
Whether the issue is a leaked exam, power cuts, or economic privation, each is refracted through the bitter, zero-sum political rivalry and tribalism among dominant political factions.
Khan has been in Adiala jail since August 2023, and sentenced again on December 20 of that year to 17 years in prison. His solitary confinement has been flagged by the U.N.’s special rapporteur on torture, and denied by the Pakistani government.
Despite being Pakistan’s most popular leader, however, Khan cannot form the center of a movement. His young supporters do not want a system repaired; they simply want a man released.
In November 2024, thousands of Khan’s supporters broke through containers and reached the edge of Islamabad’s D-Chowk. But a midnight operation by the state jailed hundreds of people. Even that protest’s larger slogans regarding the stolen mandate and the constitutional amendment rode entirely on Khan’s name. A mobilization whose single demand is the freedom of one jailed man can be beaten by keeping him jailed, which is exactly what the state did.
To be sure, Pakistan has several issue-first movements. The Baloch Yakjehti Committee that Mahrang Baloch leads organizes around the issue of enforced disappearances rather than partisan loyalties. The Pashtun rights marches, the Aurat March, the lawyers who once faced down Gen. Musharraf – none of them was a fan club.
But each of them soon hits a ceiling that the Delhi protests did not. They are read as ethnic, or provincial, or feminist, or foreign-sponsored, and limited before they can attain national salience.
The Pakistani state prefers it this way, of course. For instance, Karachi’s grievances were folded into the Mohajir Qaumi Movement and delegitimized as foreign-sponsored. National fury at the Sharif and Bhutto dynasties was muted by its association with Khan as the agent of change.
A cause cannot be contained the same way, so the establishment survives by encouraging this sort of personality politics. Today the PTI draws off nearly all the political oxygen in the country, leaving little for any other issue.
What has helped the establishment is a ban on student unions imposed by Gen. Zia-ul-Haq in 1984 that has never been lifted. A 1993 court ruling locked the ban in place, along with the affidavit that students and a parent must still sign, swearing off politics as the price of admission.
Bangladesh’s revolt was launched by a non-partisan student platform. Sri Lanka’s grew from a leaderless citizens’ movement. Nepal’s was driven by a generational mobilization that crossed party lines. Pakistan, on the otheer hand, dismantled its own independent student unions 40 years ago and let nothing grow in its place. Meanwhile, its political parties are merely vehicles for personalities.
The wall is not without a crack. Hamza Khawaja, a law graduate from Lahore University of Management Sciences, has petitioned the Supreme Court to restore the unions and strike down the pledge requirement for university admissions, and the court has put the government on notice to answer. Its outcome may not be as swift as mobilized action by a crowd, but it is the rare Pakistani fight waged over a system rather than in support of an individual savior.
When young Pakistanis stop introducing themselves as Youthia or Patwari or Jiyala, and start identifying themselves as unemployed, overcharged, or simply students – that is, when they define themselves by a condition they share rather than a leader they follow – the street will come to their support.
articles.summary: Imran Khan is undoubtedly popular. But building a protest movement that revolves around Khan and his freedom immediately excludes half the population.

articles.title: Myanmar Leader Criticizes Five-Point Consensus, Accuses ASEAN of ‘Discrimination’
articles.full_text:
Marking his 100th day as president, Min Aung Hlaing told parliament that his administration would pursue its own “solution” to the country’s conflict.
Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing addresses a joint session of parliament in Naypyidaw, Myanmar, July 31, 2026.
Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing on Friday criticized the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan, accusing member states of “discriminating” against the country.
The remarks came during a speech to a joint session of parliament marking the first 100 days since the former military chief, who led the 2021 military coup, took office at the head of a military-backed civilian administration.
“The government noted that although some ASEAN member states had, over the past five years, adopted positions and practices that it regarded as discriminatory towards Myanmar, Myanmar had exercised patience and continued to cooperate in accordance with its responsibilities as an ASEAN member state,” Min Aung Hlaing said, according to a transcript of his speech published by the Myanmar News Agency.
The Five-Point Consensus was agreed at a special ASEAN summit in Jakarta in April 2021, just over two months after the military seized power in a coup. Min Aung Hlaing attended the meeting, where ASEAN leaders agreed on five points, including the appointment of a special envoy, an immediate end to violence, access to humanitarian aid, and dialogue among “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
The military junta has done little to implement the most important points of the Consensus, instead choosing to defeat by force the groups opposing military rule, which the regime has characterized as “terrorists.” This prompted the remaining ASEAN member states to bar it from the bloc’s summits in late 2021, a restriction which remains in place.
In his speech, Min Aung Hlaing argued further that the Five-Point Consensus was “not the consensus of all ASEAN member states” and that it “was only the statement of the then ASEAN chair, Brunei.” (This remark, reported by Myanmar Now, did not appear in the Myanmar News Agency transcript.)
“The government further stated that it would respond to any discriminatory actions that are not constructive on a case-by-case basis, as necessary,” he added.
This echoed the argument made by Myanmar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs last week, when it declared that the Consensus “was attached as an annex” to a statement by the ASEAN chair, “without prior notification and circulation of a draft” to member states. It was therefore “released without reaching a consensus among all Member States.”
Since being anointed president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has pushed hard for full readmission to ASEAN – even as his administration has become more defiant about the Five-Point Consensus. Earlier this month, Myanmar’s pro-military parliament adopted a motion rejecting the Consensus as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs, and that it “does not align with the current political developments in Myanmar.” In its statement last week, the Foreign Ministry said last week that the government was “obliged to respect” the motion.
ASEAN has shown a greater willingness to engage with Myanmar, and member states like Thailand have advocated bringing it back into the “ASEAN family” – but Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, the current ASEAN special envoy for Myanmar, says that this would require genuine attempts to implement the Five-Point Consensus. Lazaro said last week that Myanmar’s full reintegration with ASEAN was “still far off” due to its lack of compliance with the bloc’s agreement.
Min Aung Hlaing’s comments confirm his government’s determination to pursue its own “solution” to the country’s conflict, which the former general outlined in detail during the course of his speech.
“The government will spend the first two years laying the groundwork and building momentum for the new nation, followed by three years dedicated to accelerating its nation-building efforts,” he said.
The administration will continue to strengthen the power of the armed forces, and will set up a “people’s militia” to help ensure “internal security,” Min Aung Hlaing said. He added that the new-look administration had invited ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) to take part in talks without preconditions and “has so far held discussions with 13 EAOs.”
The administration plans next year to hold by-elections in 172 constituencies that were unable to vote during the three-phase elections held in December and January, and outlined plans to develop the agriculture, education, and tourism sectors.
A key focus of the coming years, Min Aung Hlaing said, was infrastructure development. In particular, he mentioned the Mandalay-Muse railway, linking central Myanmar to the Chinese border, which he said would “greatly enhance Myanmar-China trade and economic cooperation” and an India-Myanmar-Thailand trilateral highway project. He said that the government is currently ​working on 10 power ⁠generation projects, including the controversial Myitsone dam in Kachin State, while pledging to continue efforts “toward the construction of a nuclear power plant.”
